title: 2  Linear Regression
text:
2.6 Categorical predictors



The lm() function can handle both numerical and categorical variables. To understand what happens if the predictor is categorical, we’ll use another data set here, PlantGrowth (type ?PlantGrowth or F1 help if you want details). We visualize the data via:

boxplot(weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth)









2.6.1 Understanding contrasts
Let’s fit an lm() now with the categorical explanatory variable group. The syntax is the same as before

fit = lm(weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth)
summary(fit)


Call:
lm(formula = weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-1.0710 -0.4180 -0.0060  0.2627  1.3690 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)   5.0320     0.1971  25.527   <2e-16 ***
grouptrt1    -0.3710     0.2788  -1.331   0.1944    
grouptrt2     0.4940     0.2788   1.772   0.0877 .  
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.6234 on 27 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.2641,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.2096 
F-statistic: 4.846 on 2 and 27 DF,  p-value: 0.01591


but the interpretation of the results often leads to confusion. We see effects for trt1 and trt2, but where is ctrl? The answer is: R is calculating so-called treatment contrasts for categorical predictors. In treatment contrasts, we have a reference level (in our case ctrl), which is the intercept of the model, and then we estimate the difference to the reference for all other factor levels (in our case trt1 and trt2).






Tip



By default, R orders factors levels alphabetically, and thus the factor level that is first in the alphabet will be used as reference level in lm(). In our example, ctrl is before trt in the alphabet and thus used as reference, which also makes sense, because it is scientifically logical to compare treatments to the control. In other cases, it may be that the logical reference level does not correspond to the alphabetical order of the factors. If you want to change which factor level is the reference, you can re-order your factor using the relevel() function. In this case, estimates and p-values will change, because different comparisons (contrasts) are being made, but model predictions will stay the same! Also, avoid choosing a reference level with very few observations: all other estimates are differences to this level, so they will all be imprecise.


This also becomes clear if we plot the results.

plot(allEffects(fit))








Note that in this case, the effects package depicts the CI by purple error bars.
So, in our example, the intercept estimates the mean weight in the ctrl group (with a p-value tested against zero, usually not interesting), and the effects of trt1 and trt2 are the differences of weight compared to the control, with a p-value for a test against an effect size of zero.






Tip 2.1: More details on contrasts





Treatment contrasts are not the only option to deal with categorical variables. A simple alternative is to remove the intercept:

fit = lm(weight ~ 0 + group, data = PlantGrowth)
summary(fit)


Call:
lm(formula = weight ~ 0 + group, data = PlantGrowth)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-1.0710 -0.4180 -0.0060  0.2627  1.3690 

Coefficients:
          Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
groupctrl   5.0320     0.1971   25.53   <2e-16 ***
grouptrt1   4.6610     0.1971   23.64   <2e-16 ***
grouptrt2   5.5260     0.1971   28.03   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.6234 on 27 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.9867,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.9852 
F-statistic: 665.5 on 3 and 27 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


This results in fitting the mean for each factor level (cell means), with p-values for a test of each mean against zero. Unfortunately, this syntax option doesn’t generalize to multiple regressions.
More generally, the coding of a factor is controlled by its contrasts. The coding never changes the fitted model (predictions, residuals, R² stay the same); it only changes what the intercept and the coefficients mean. For PlantGrowth (group means ctrl = 5.03, trt1 = 4.66, trt2 = 5.53; average of the means \(\bar\mu\) = 5.07), the common codings give:









Coding (R)
Intercept
Coefficients
Typical use




Treatment (contr.treatment, default)
\(\mu_1\) = 5.03
\(\mu_2-\mu_1\), \(\mu_3-\mu_1\)
regression tables, comparison to a control


Sum-to-zero (contr.sum)
\(\bar\mu\) = 5.07
\(\mu_1-\bar\mu\), \(\mu_2-\bar\mu\)
type III ANOVA, effects averaged over levels


Helmert (contr.helmert)
\(\bar\mu\) = 5.07
\((\mu_2-\mu_1)/2\), \((\mu_3-(\mu_1+\mu_2)/2)/3\)
sequential comparisons (note the scaling)


Polynomial (contr.poly)
\(\bar\mu\) = 5.07
linear and quadratic trend (scaled)
ordered levels (ordered() uses this)



You can set the contrasts for a factor, or locally in the model call:

fit = lm(weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth,
         contrasts = list(group = contr.helmert))
summary(fit)


Call:
lm(formula = weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth, contrasts = list(group = contr.helmert))

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-1.0710 -0.4180 -0.0060  0.2627  1.3690 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  5.07300    0.11381  44.573  < 2e-16 ***
group1      -0.18550    0.13939  -1.331  0.19439    
group2       0.22650    0.08048   2.814  0.00901 ** 
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.6234 on 27 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.2641,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.2096 
F-statistic: 4.846 on 2 and 27 DF,  p-value: 0.01591


Note that the Helmert coefficients are scaled: -0.19 is half the difference between trt1 and ctrl. Polynomial contrasts assume equally spaced levels; if your levels are e.g. doses of 1, 2 and 5, use contr.poly(3, scores = c(1, 2, 5)).
Sum-to-zero vs. orthogonal contrasts. Two properties of contrasts are often confused. Sum-to-zero means that each contrast column sums to zero over the factor levels. Then the intercept is the unweighted average of the group means, and in models with interactions, main effects are averages over the levels of the other factor; this is the property a type III ANOVA requires (see Section 3.2.4). Orthogonal contrasts are sum-to-zero contrasts whose columns are, in addition, uncorrelated with each other. You can see both properties in the cross-product of the coding matrix, including a column for the intercept: zeros in the first row mean sum-to-zero, zeros between the other columns mean orthogonal:

crossprod(cbind(intercept = 1, contr.sum(3)))

          intercept    
intercept         3 0 0
                  0 2 1
                  0 1 2

crossprod(cbind(intercept = 1, contr.helmert(3)))

          intercept    
intercept         3 0 0
                  0 2 0
                  0 0 6


Thus, contr.sum sums to zero but is not orthogonal, while Helmert and polynomial contrasts are both (which is why all three have the same intercept in the table above). For a type III ANOVA, sum-to-zero is enough: all sum-to-zero codings give the same results. Orthogonality matters if you want to split the sum of squares of a factor into independent parts (see planned comparisons below), and only translates into independent estimates if the group sizes are equal. Treatment contrasts do not sum to zero, and are therefore no contrasts in this strict sense.
Planned comparisons. If you have specific hypotheses, e.g. “do the treatments differ from the control?” and “do the two treatments differ from each other?”, you can test them as custom contrasts. Don’t write the weights of your hypotheses directly into contrasts(): this only gives the intended tests if the contrasts are mutually orthogonal and the design is balanced. The safer route is the emmeans package, where you specify the weights of each hypothesis on the group means directly:

library(emmeans)
emm = emmeans(lm(weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth), ~ group)
contrast(emm, list(ctrl_vs_trt = c(-1, 0.5, 0.5),
                   trt1_vs_trt2 = c(0, -1, 1)))

 contrast     estimate    SE df t.ratio p.value
 ctrl_vs_trt    0.0615 0.241 27   0.255  0.8009
 trt1_vs_trt2   0.8650 0.279 27   3.103  0.0045


The two contrasts here are orthogonal (the products of their weights sum to zero) and the design is balanced. In this case, their sums of squares add up exactly to the sum of squares of the factor in the ANOVA, which you can see with the split argument of summary.aov():

PlantGrowth$group2 = PlantGrowth$group
contrasts(PlantGrowth$group2) = cbind(ctrl_vs_trt = c(-2, 1, 1),
                                      trt1_vs_trt2 = c(0, -1, 1))
summary(aov(weight ~ group2, data = PlantGrowth),
        split = list(group2 = list(ctrl_vs_trt = 1, trt1_vs_trt2 = 2)))

                       Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value  Pr(>F)   
group2                  2  3.766   1.883   4.846 0.01591 * 
  group2: ctrl_vs_trt   1  0.025   0.025   0.065 0.80086   
  group2: trt1_vs_trt2  1  3.741   3.741   9.627 0.00446 **
Residuals              27 10.492   0.389                   
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


With unequal group sizes, the parts still add up (the split is sequential), but the result now depends on the order of the contrasts. Note also that orthogonal contrasts do not protect against multiple testing. Planned comparisons should be defined before seeing the data, and you should decide in advance if and how you correct for multiple testing.
For more details, see Schad et al. (2020), chapter 10 in the book by Berg (2025) and also Schielzeth (2010).




Berg, S.M. van den (2025) Analysing data using linear models: With applications in R. bookdown.org. Available at: https://bookdown.org/pingapang9/linear_models_bookdown/ (Accessed: October 3, 2026).

Schad, D.J. et al. (2020) “How to capitalize on a priori contrasts in linear (mixed) models: A tutorial,” Journal of Memory and Language, 110, p. 104038. Available at: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jml.2019.104038.

How the coding affects the ANOVA, in particular the type III ANOVA in models with interactions, is discussed in the section on contrasts and ANOVA results (Section 3.2.4).



2.6.2 ANOVA
For categorical predictors, one nearly always performs an ANOVA on top of the linear regression estimates. The underlying ideas behind this will be explained in more detail in the section on the idea of ANOVA (Section 3.1), but just very quickly:
An ANOVA starts with a base model (in this case intercept only) and adds the variable group. It then measures:

How much the model improves in terms of \({R}^{2}\) (this is in the column Sum Sq).
If this increase of model fit is significant.

We can run an ANOVA on the fitted model object using aov(). Note that we use aov() here rather than the more common anova(fit), because the post-hoc test TukeyHSD() used below requires an aov object as input:

fit = lm(weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth)
anov = aov(fit)
summary(anov)

            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value Pr(>F)  
group        2  3.766  1.8832   4.846 0.0159 *
Residuals   27 10.492  0.3886                 
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


In this case, we would conclude that the variable group (3 levels) significantly improves model fit, i.e. the group overall has a significant effect, even though the individual contrasts in the original model were not significant.






Note



The situation that the ANOVA is significant, but the linear regression contrasts are not, is often perceived as confusing, but this is perfectly normal and not a contradiction.
The ANOVA tests a different hypothesis (at least one group mean differs) than the individual coefficients (each treatment vs the reference). In the summary of a lm(), for >2 levels, not all possible contrasts are tested: in our example, we estimate p-values for ctrl-trt1 and ctrl-trt2, which are both n.s., but we do not test for differences of trt1-trt2 (which happens to be significant). The largest difference is between trt1 and trt2; therefore the omnibus test can be significant although both treatment-vs-control contrasts are not.
Thus, the general idea is: 1. ANOVA tells us if there is an effect of the variable at all, 2. summary() tests for specific group differences.




2.6.3 Post-hoc tests
Another common test performed on top of an ANOVA or a categorical predictor of an lm() is a so-called post-hoc test. Basically, a post-hoc test computes p-values for all possible combinations of factor levels, usually corrected for multiple testing:

TukeyHSD(anov)

  Tukey multiple comparisons of means
    95% family-wise confidence level

Fit: aov(formula = fit)

$group
            diff        lwr       upr     p adj
trt1-ctrl -0.371 -1.0622161 0.3202161 0.3908711
trt2-ctrl  0.494 -0.1972161 1.1852161 0.1979960
trt2-trt1  0.865  0.1737839 1.5562161 0.0120064


In the result, we see, as hinted at in Section 2.6.2, that there is a significant difference between trt1 and trt2. Note that the p-values of the post-hoc tests are larger than those of the lm summary(). This is because post-hoc tests nearly always correct p-values for multiple testing, while regression estimates are usually not corrected for multiple testing (you could of course if you wanted).






Note



Remember: a significance test with a significance threshold of alpha = 0.05 has a type I error rate of 5%. Thus, if you make 20 independent tests, you would expect about one significant result by chance (probability of at least one: 1 - 0.95^20, about 64%), even if there are no effects whatsoever. Corrections for multiple testing are used to compensate for this, usually aiming at controlling the family-wise error rate (FWER), the probability of making one or more type I errors when performing multiple hypotheses tests. For any set of p-values, p.adjust(p, method = "holm") (FWER) or p.adjust(p, method = "BH") (false discovery rate) applies such a correction; the family of tests is defined by the question the analysis answers.


TukeyHSD() only works for simple ANOVA models fitted with aov(). A more general alternative is the emmeans package, which works for lm, glm and mixed models, and also for models with several predictors. emmeans() calculates the estimated mean for each factor level, and pairs() compares all of them, with Tukey adjustment as default:

library(emmeans)
fit = lm(weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth)
emm = emmeans(fit, ~ group)
emm

 group emmean    SE df lower.CL upper.CL
 ctrl    5.03 0.197 27     4.63     5.44
 trt1    4.66 0.197 27     4.26     5.07
 trt2    5.53 0.197 27     5.12     5.93

Confidence level used: 0.95 

pairs(emm)

 contrast    estimate    SE df t.ratio p.value
 ctrl - trt1    0.371 0.279 27   1.331  0.3909
 ctrl - trt2   -0.494 0.279 27  -1.772  0.1980
 trt1 - trt2   -0.865 0.279 27  -3.103  0.0120

P value adjustment: tukey method for comparing a family of 3 estimates 


If you are only interested in comparing each treatment against a control, you make fewer comparisons, and thus have more power. This is the so-called Dunnett test:

contrast(emm, "trt.vs.ctrl", ref = "ctrl")

 contrast    estimate    SE df t.ratio p.value
 trt1 - ctrl   -0.371 0.279 27  -1.331  0.3296
 trt2 - ctrl    0.494 0.279 27   1.772  0.1582

P value adjustment: dunnettx method for 2 tests 


Make sure to name the control with ref; otherwise, the first factor level is used as control. The default adjustment for this test (dunnettx) is an approximation; for exact p-values, add adjust = "mvt". We will use emmeans more extensively in the chapter on ANOVA (Chapter 3; see in particular Note 3.1).


2.6.4 Compact letter display
It is common to visualize the results of the post-hoc tests with the so-called Compact Letter Display (cld). This doesn’t work with the base TukeyHSD function, so we will use the multcomp package:

library(multcomp)

fit = lm(weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth)
tuk = glht(fit, linfct = mcp(group = "Tukey"))
summary(tuk)          # Standard display.


     Simultaneous Tests for General Linear Hypotheses

Multiple Comparisons of Means: Tukey Contrasts


Fit: lm(formula = weight ~ group, data = PlantGrowth)

Linear Hypotheses:
                 Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)  
trt1 - ctrl == 0  -0.3710     0.2788  -1.331   0.3909  
trt2 - ctrl == 0   0.4940     0.2788   1.772   0.1979  
trt2 - trt1 == 0   0.8650     0.2788   3.103   0.0119 *
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
(Adjusted p values reported -- single-step method)

tuk.cld = cld(tuk)    # Letter-based display.
plot(tuk.cld)

The cld gives a new letter for each group of factor levels that are statistically undistinguishable. You can see the output via tuk.cld, here I only show the plot:

title: 2  Linear Regression
text:
2.7 Specifying a multiple regression



Multiple (linear) regression means that we consider more than 1 predictor in the same model. The syntax is very easy: Just add your predictors (numerical or categorical) to your regression formula, as in the following example for the airquality dataset. To be able to also add a factor, I created a new variable fMonth to have month as a factor (categorical):

airquality$fMonth = factor(airquality$Month)
fit = lm(Ozone ~ Temp + Wind + Solar.R + fMonth, data = airquality)

In principle, everything is interpreted as before: First of all, residual plots:

par(mfrow =c(2,2))
plot(fit)














Tip



Maybe you have noted that the residual plots used fitted values as the x axis. This is in general the most parsimonious choice, as there are many predictors in a multiple regression, and each influences the response. However, if running a multiple regression, you should additionally plot residuals against each predictor separately - if doing so, you often see a misfit that doesn’t occur in the res ~ predicted plot.


The resulting regression table already looks a bit intimidating,

summary(fit)


Call:
lm(formula = Ozone ~ Temp + Wind + Solar.R + fMonth, data = airquality)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-40.344 -13.495  -3.165  10.399  92.689 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) -74.23481   26.10184  -2.844  0.00537 ** 
Temp          1.87511    0.34073   5.503 2.74e-07 ***
Wind         -3.10872    0.66009  -4.710 7.78e-06 ***
Solar.R       0.05222    0.02367   2.206  0.02957 *  
fMonth6     -14.75895    9.12269  -1.618  0.10876    
fMonth7      -8.74861    7.82906  -1.117  0.26640    
fMonth8      -4.19654    8.14693  -0.515  0.60758    
fMonth9     -15.96728    6.65561  -2.399  0.01823 *  
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 20.72 on 103 degrees of freedom
  (42 observations deleted due to missingness)
Multiple R-squared:  0.6369,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.6122 
F-statistic: 25.81 on 7 and 103 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Luckily, we also have the effect plots to make sense of this:

library(effects)
plot(allEffects(fit, partial.residuals = T) )














Tip



Note that for the multiple regression, that scatter around the regression line displayed by the effects package is not the raw data, but the so-called partial residuals. Essentially, what this means is that we plot the fitted line for the respective predictor, and then we calculate the residual for the full model (including the other predictors) and add them on the regression line. The advantage is that this subtracts the effect of other predictors, so the scatter shows the part of the response not explained by the other predictors, i.e. the conditional effect of this predictor (see Section 2.8 for collinearity).



Formula syntax







Formula
Meaning
Details




y~x_1
\(y=a_0 +a_1*x_1\)
Slope+Intercept


y~x_1 - 1
\(y=a_1*x_1\)
Slope, no intercept


y~I(x_1^2)
\(y=a_0 + a_1*(x_1^2)\)
Quadratic effect


y~x_1+x_2
\(y=a_0+a_1*x_1+a_2*x_2\)
Multiple linear regression (two variables)


y~x_1:x_2
\(y=a_0+a_1*(x_1*x_2)\)
Interaction between x1 and x2


y~x_1*x_2
\(y=a_0+a_1*x_1+a_2*x_2+a_3*(x_1*x_2)\)
Interaction and main effects

title: 2  Linear Regression
text:
2.8 The effect of collinearity



A common misunderstanding is that a multiple regression is just a convenient way to run several independent univariate regressions. This, however, is wrong. A multiple regression is doing a fundamentally different thing. Let’s compare the results of the multiple regression in Section 2.7 to the simple regression.

fit = lm(Ozone ~ Wind , data = airquality)
summary(fit)


Call:
lm(formula = Ozone ~ Wind, data = airquality)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-51.572 -18.854  -4.868  15.234  90.000 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  96.8729     7.2387   13.38  < 2e-16 ***
Wind         -5.5509     0.6904   -8.04 9.27e-13 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 26.47 on 114 degrees of freedom
  (37 observations deleted due to missingness)
Multiple R-squared:  0.3619,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.3563 
F-statistic: 64.64 on 1 and 114 DF,  p-value: 9.272e-13


The simple regression estimates an effect of Wind that is -5.55, while in the multiple regression, we had -3.1.
The reason is that a multiple regression estimates the effect of Wind, corrected for the effect of the other variables, while a univariate regression estimates the raw correlation of Ozone and Wind. And this can make a big difference if Wind has correlations with other variables(the technical term is collinear). We can see, e.g., that Wind and Temp are indeed correlated by running

plot(Wind ~ Temp, data = airquality)










How to quantify collinearity? For two predictors, their correlation (cor()) is sufficient (|r| > 0.7 is a common warning sign). With more predictors, variance inflation factors (car::vif(fit) on the fitted model) are more informative: they also detect a predictor that is well explained by a combination of the others, and √VIF is the factor by which its standard error is inflated. As a rough guide, values above 5–10 are often considered problematic.
In such a case, if Temp is not included in the regression, the effect of Temp will be absorbed in the Wind effect to the extent to which both variables are collinear. In other words, if one variable is missing, there will be a spillover of the effect of this variable to all collinear variables. This spillover is omitted-variable bias, the core of confounding; whether adding a variable to the regression is the right thing to do depends on the causal structure (colliders, mediators), see Chapter 7.






Tip



To give a simple example of this spillover, let’s say

Wind has a positive effect of 1
Temp has a negative effect of -1
Wind and Temp are correlated 50%

A multiple regression would estimate 1,-1. In a single regression of the response on Wind alone (with Wind and Temp standardized and correlated at 0.5), the collinear part of the Temp effect would be absorbed by Wind, so we would estimate a Wind effect of 1 + (-1)(0.5) = 0.5.


Note that the same happens in univariate plots of the correlation, i.e. this is not a problem of the linear regression, but rather of looking at the univariate correlation of Ozone ~ Wind without correcting for the effect of Temp.
Also, note that collinearity is not fundamentally a problem for the regression - regression estimates stay unbiased and p-values and CIs calibrated under arbitrary high collinearity. However, the more collinearity we have, the more uncertain regression estimates will become (with associated large p-values). Here an example, where we simulate data under the assumption that x1 and x2 have each an effect of 1

set.seed(123)
x1 = runif(100)
x2 = 0.95 *x1 + 0.05 * runif(100)
y = x1 + x2 + rnorm(100)

summary(lm(y ~ x1 + x2))


Call:
lm(formula = y ~ x1 + x2)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-1.8994 -0.6821 -0.1086  0.5749  3.3663 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)  -0.1408     0.2862  -0.492    0.624
x1            1.6605     7.0742   0.235    0.815
x2            0.4072     7.4695   0.055    0.957

Residual standard error: 0.9765 on 97 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.2668,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.2517 
F-statistic: 17.65 on 2 and 97 DF,  p-value: 2.91e-07


We see that the multiple regression is not terribly wrong, but very uncertain about the true values. Some authors therefore advise to remove collinear predictors (for an overview of methods to deal with collinearity, see Dormann et al., 2013). This can sometimes be useful, in particular for predictions (see the bias-variance trade-off, Section 8.1); however, note that the effect of the removed predictor will then be absorbed by the remaining predictor(s). In our case, the univariate regression would be very sure that there is an effect, note that the CI does not cover the true effect of x1 (which was 1).

Dormann, C.F. et al. (2013) “Collinearity: A review of methods to deal with it and a simulation study evaluating their performance,” Ecography, 36(1), pp. 27–46. Available at: https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1600-0587.2012.07348.x.

summary(lm(y ~ x1))


Call:
lm(formula = y ~ x1)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-1.9000 -0.6757 -0.1067  0.5799  3.3630 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  -0.1295     0.1965  -0.659    0.511    
x1            2.0456     0.3426   5.971 3.78e-08 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.9715 on 98 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.2668,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.2593 
F-statistic: 35.65 on 1 and 98 DF,  p-value: 3.785e-08








TipUnderstanding collinearity spillover in more detail





We can understand the problem of one variable influencing the effect of the other in more detail if we simulate some data. Let’s create 2 positively collinear predictors:

x1 = runif(100, -5, 5)
x2 = x1 + 0.2*runif(100, -5, 5)

We can check whether this has worked:

cor(x1, x2)

[1] 0.9810774


Now, the first case I want to look at, is when the effects for x1 and x2 have equal signs. Let’s create such a situation, by simulating a normal response \(y\), where the intercept is 0, and both predictors have effect = 1:

y = 0 + 1*x1 + 1*x2 + rnorm(100)

If you look at the formula, you can nearly visually see what the problem of the univariate regression is: as x2 is nearly identical to x1, the apparent slope between y and either x1 or x2 will be around 2 (although the true effect is 1).
Consequently, the univariate models will estimate too high effect sizes. We also say by taking out one predictor, the remaining one is absorbing the effect of the other predictor.

coef(lm(y ~ x1))

(Intercept)          x1 
0.002362246 2.003283129 

coef(lm(y ~ x2))

(Intercept)          x2 
-0.08366353  1.91355593 


The multivariate model, on the other hand, gets the right estimates (with a bit of error):

coef(lm(y~x1 + x2))

(Intercept)          x1          x2 
-0.03627352  1.05770683  0.92146207 


You can also see this visually:

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(x1, y, main = "x1 effect", ylim = c(-12, 12))
abline(lm(y ~ x1))

# Draw a line with intercept 0 and slope 1,
# just like we simulated the true dependency of y on x1:
abline(0, 1, col = "red")

legend("topleft", c("fitted", "true"), lwd = 1, col = c("black", "red"))
plot(x2, y, main = "x2 effect", ylim = c(-12, 12))
abline(lm(y ~ x2))
abline(0, 1, col = "red")
legend("topleft", c("fitted", "true"), lwd = 1, col = c("black", "red"))








Check what happens if the two predictors are negatively correlated (both effects are still 1).

x1 = runif(100, -5, 5)
x2 = -x1 + 0.2*runif(100, -5, 5)
y = 0 + 1*x1 + 1*x2 + rnorm(100)

cor(x1, x2)

[1] -0.9804515

coef(lm(y ~ x1))

(Intercept)          x1 
-0.03467159 -0.01170653 

coef(lm(y ~ x2))

(Intercept)          x2 
-0.04036562  0.04795055 

par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
plot(x1, y, main = "x1 effect", ylim = c(-12, 12))
abline(lm(y ~ x1))
abline(0, 1, col = "red")
legend("topleft", c("fitted", "true"), lwd = 1, col = c("black", "red"))
plot(x2, y, main = "x2 effect", ylim = c(-12, 12))
abline(lm(y ~ x2))
abline(0, 1, col = "red")
legend("topleft", c("fitted", "true"), lwd = 1, col = c("black", "red"))







coef(lm(y~x1 + x2))

(Intercept)          x1          x2 
-0.04622019  0.91103840  0.94186191 


In the univariate regressions, the two effects cancel out (slopes close to 0), while the multiple regression recovers both effects.

title: 2  Linear Regression
section: 2.9 Centering and scaling of predictor variables
text:
2.9 Centering and scaling of predictor variables




2.9.1 Centering
In our multiple regression (Section 2.7), we saw an intercept of -74. Per definition, the intercept is the predicted value for \(y\) (Ozone) at a value of 0 for all other variables. It’s fine to report this, as long as we are interested in this value, but often the value at predictor = 0 is not particularly interesting. In this specific case, a value of -74 clearly doesn’t make sense, as Ozone concentrations can only be positive.
To explain what’s going on, let’s look at the univariate regression against Temp:

fit = lm(Ozone ~ Temp, data = airquality)
summary(fit)


Call:
lm(formula = Ozone ~ Temp, data = airquality)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-40.729 -17.409  -0.587  11.306 118.271 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) -146.9955    18.2872  -8.038 9.37e-13 ***
Temp           2.4287     0.2331  10.418  < 2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 23.71 on 114 degrees of freedom
  (37 observations deleted due to missingness)
Multiple R-squared:  0.4877,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.4832 
F-statistic: 108.5 on 1 and 114 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


Now, the intercept is -147. We can see the reason more clearly when we plot the results:

plot(Ozone ~ Temp, data = airquality, xlim = c(-10, 110), ylim = c(-200, 170))
abline(fit)
abline(h = 0, lty = 2)
abline(v = 0, lty = 2)








That shows us that the value 0 is far outside of the set of our observed values for Temp, which is measured in Fahrenheit. Thus, we are extrapolating the Ozone far beyond the observed data. To avoid this, we can simply re-define the x-Axis, by subtracting the mean, which is called centering:

airquality$cTemp = airquality$Temp - mean(airquality$Temp)

Alternatively, you can center with the built-in R command scale

airquality$cTemp = scale(airquality$Temp, center = T, scale = F)







Tipscale() returns a matrix that remembers the transformation



scale() returns a one-column matrix that stores the values used for the transformation as attributes: attr(airquality$cTemp, "scaled:center") gives the mean that was subtracted (77.9), and if you also scale (see Section 2.9.2), "scaled:scale" gives the standard deviation that was divided by. This is useful to translate results back to the original units, e.g. the estimate for a scaled predictor divided by attr(x, "scaled:scale") is the effect per original unit. The downside is that some functions expect plain numeric columns. For example, predict() with newdata stops with the error ‘variable … was fitted with type “nmatrix.1” but type “numeric” was supplied’ if you supply plain numbers for such a variable. In this case, transform the new values in the same way, e.g. scale(newdata$Temp, center = attr(airquality$cTemp, "scaled:center"), scale = FALSE) (for a scaled variable, also pass scale = attr(..., "scaled:scale")). Some other functions (e.g. from the effects package) convert such columns to plain vectors and print a warning about it, which is harmless.


Fitting the model with the centered variable moves the intercept line in the middle of the predictor range

fit = lm(Ozone ~ cTemp, data = airquality)
plot(Ozone ~ cTemp, data = airquality)
abline(fit)
abline(v = 0, lty = 2)








which produces a more interpretable value for the intercept: when we center, the intercept of the centered variable can be interpreted as the Ozone concentration at the mean temperature. For a univariate regression, this value will also typically be very similar to the grand mean mean(airquality$Ozone, na.rm = TRUE) (42.1).

summary(fit)


Call:
lm(formula = Ozone ~ cTemp, data = airquality)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-40.729 -17.409  -0.587  11.306 118.271 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  42.1576     2.2018   19.15   <2e-16 ***
cTemp         2.4287     0.2331   10.42   <2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 23.71 on 114 degrees of freedom
  (37 observations deleted due to missingness)
Multiple R-squared:  0.4877,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.4832 
F-statistic: 108.5 on 1 and 114 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16








Caution



For categorical predictors, the analog of centering is sum-to-zero coding (contr.sum, see Section 2.6.1): the intercept is then the average over the levels. With the default treatment contrasts, the intercept is predicted for the reference group of all categorical variables, evaluated at the mean of all numeric variables (if centered). Random effects also estimate a grand mean over all groups (see Section 4.3.1).




2.9.2 Scaling
Another very common transformation is to divide the x axis by a certain value to bring all variables on a similar scale. This is called scaling.
The main motivation for scaling is to make effect sizes in a multiple regression more comparable. As an example, look again at the multiple regression with 4 predictors (Section 2.7):

airquality$fMonth = factor(airquality$Month)
fit = lm(Ozone ~ Temp + Wind + Solar.R + fMonth, data = airquality)
summary(fit)


Call:
lm(formula = Ozone ~ Temp + Wind + Solar.R + fMonth, data = airquality)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-40.344 -13.495  -3.165  10.399  92.689 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) -74.23481   26.10184  -2.844  0.00537 ** 
Temp          1.87511    0.34073   5.503 2.74e-07 ***
Wind         -3.10872    0.66009  -4.710 7.78e-06 ***
Solar.R       0.05222    0.02367   2.206  0.02957 *  
fMonth6     -14.75895    9.12269  -1.618  0.10876    
fMonth7      -8.74861    7.82906  -1.117  0.26640    
fMonth8      -4.19654    8.14693  -0.515  0.60758    
fMonth9     -15.96728    6.65561  -2.399  0.01823 *  
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 20.72 on 103 degrees of freedom
  (42 observations deleted due to missingness)
Multiple R-squared:  0.6369,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.6122 
F-statistic: 25.81 on 7 and 103 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


So, which of the predictors is the strongest (= largest effect on the response)? Superficially, it looks as if Month has the highest values. But we have to remember that the effect on the response is \(y = \text{regression estimate} * \text{predictor}\), i.e if we have a predictor with a large range (difference between min/max values), it may have a strong effect even though the estimate is small. So, if the predictors have a different range, we cannot compare effect sizes directly regarding their “effective influence” on y.
To make the effect sizes comparable, we can scale all numeric predictors by dividing them by their standard deviation, which will bring them all roughly on a range between -2, 2. You can do this by hand, or use the scale() function in R:






Tip



By default, the scale(...) function will scale and center. As discussed in Section 2.9.1, centering is nearly always useful as it improves the interpretability of the intercept, so I would suggest to use this as a default when scaling.



airquality$sTemp = scale(airquality$Temp)
airquality$sWind = scale(airquality$Wind)
airquality$sSolar.R = scale(airquality$Solar.R)

These are one-column matrices that keep their mean and standard deviation as attributes (see the tip box in Section 2.9.1).






Tip



Here, I create a new variable for each scaled predictor. It is possible to use the scale() command inside the regression formula as well, but that sometimes creates problems with downstream plotting functions, so I recommend to create a new variable in your data for scaling.


Running the regression:

fit = lm(Ozone ~ sTemp + sWind + sSolar.R + fMonth, data = airquality)
summary(fit)


Call:
lm(formula = Ozone ~ sTemp + sWind + sSolar.R + fMonth, data = airquality)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-40.344 -13.495  -3.165  10.399  92.689 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)   50.558      5.526   9.150 5.74e-15 ***
sTemp         17.748      3.225   5.503 2.74e-07 ***
sWind        -10.952      2.325  -4.710 7.78e-06 ***
sSolar.R       4.703      2.131   2.206   0.0296 *  
fMonth6      -14.759      9.123  -1.618   0.1088    
fMonth7       -8.749      7.829  -1.117   0.2664    
fMonth8       -4.197      8.147  -0.515   0.6076    
fMonth9      -15.967      6.656  -2.399   0.0182 *  
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 20.72 on 103 degrees of freedom
  (42 observations deleted due to missingness)
Multiple R-squared:  0.6369,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.6122 
F-statistic: 25.81 on 7 and 103 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


As you see, effect sizes have now changed considerably. The difference in interpretation is the following: for the unscaled variables, we estimate the effect of 1 unit change (e.g. 1 degree for temp). For the scaled variable, we estimate the effect of a change of 1 standard deviation. If we look at the sd of temperature

sd(airquality$Temp)

[1] 9.46527


we can conclude that the scaled regression is estimating an effect of a 9.46527 degree change in temperature.
While the latter is numerically a bit confusing, the advantage is that so we can interpret the Ozone effect scaled to typical temperature differences in the data, and the same for all other variables. Consequently, it makes sense to compare the scaled effect sizes between variables, which suggests, judged by the point estimates, that Temp is the most important predictor (check the CIs before ranking).
What about categorical variables, do we need to scale them as well? The answer is no, because they are effectively already scaled to a range of 1, because in the standard contrasts (treatment effects), we estimate the effect of going from option 1 to option 2. However, note that because scaling by 1 sd gives numeric predictors a typical range of about +/-1 sd, i.e. 2 sd in total, some authors also scale by 2 sd, so that numeric and categorical variables are more comparable in their effect sizes.






CautionExercise — Discuss centering



Under which circumstances should you center / scale, and how should you discuss the estimated coefficients in a paper?








TipSolution





Scaling: scaled, you get estimate of relative importance, while unscaled, effects are interpretable in their original units. Depending on what you are more interested in, you may report one of the two, or both. Centering: changes the place of the origin, and thus the interpretation of the intercept (and possibly also main effects if interactions are present, see Section 2.10.3). Per default, I would scale.









CautionExercise



How does adding a constant to, or multiplying, the predictor change the intercept and slope (effect, CI, p-values) of a regression?








TipSolution





Original model

fit = lm(Ozone ~ Temp, data = airquality)
summary(fit)

(Intercept) -146.9955    18.2872  -8.038 9.37e-13 ***
Temp           2.4287     0.2331  10.418  < 2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

  (37 observations deleted due to missingness)

F-statistic: 108.5 on 1 and 114 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

summary(fit)


Call:
lm(formula = Ozone ~ I(Temp + 100), data = airquality)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-40.729 -17.409  -0.587  11.306 118.271 

Coefficients:

(Intercept)   -389.8658    41.5257  -9.389 7.39e-16 ***
I(Temp + 100)    2.4287     0.2331  10.418  < 2e-16 ***
---

Adding a constant c to the predictor changes only the intercept (by minus c times the slope, here -100 * 2.43 = -243). Slope, SE, CI and p-value stay the same; only the test of the intercept changes, because it refers to a different point.

fit = lm(Ozone ~ I(Temp * 10), data = airquality)
summary(fit)


Call:
lm(formula = Ozone ~ I(Temp * 10), data = airquality)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-40.729 -17.409  -0.587  11.306 118.271 

Coefficients:

(Intercept)  -146.99549   18.28717  -8.038 9.37e-13 ***
I(Temp * 10)    0.24287    0.02331  10.418  < 2e-16 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

  (37 observations deleted due to missingness)

Multiplying the predictor by k divides the slope and its SE by k (here 2.43 becomes 0.243), so t-value and p-value stay the same; the intercept is unchanged. Combinations of both have both effects together.

title: 2  Linear Regression
text:
2.10 Interactions




2.10.1 Syntax
When we have multiple variables, we can have the situation that the value of one variable influences the effect of the other(s). Technically, this is called an interaction. In situations where the causal direction is known, this is also called a moderator. An example: Imagine we observe that the effect of aspirin differs depending on the weight of the subject. Technically, we have an interaction between aspirin and weight. Physiologically, we know the causal direction is “weight -> effect of aspirin”, so we can say weight is a moderator for the effect of aspirin.

fit = lm(Ozone ~ Temp * Wind, data = airquality)
plot(allEffects(fit))








We will have a look at the summary later, but for the moment, let’s just look at the output visually. In the effect plots, we see the effect of Temperature on Ozone for different values of Wind. We also see that the slope changes. For low Wind, we have a strong effect of Temperature. For high Wind, the effect is basically gone.
Let’s look at the interaction syntax in more detail. The “*” operator in an lm() is a shorthand for main effects + interactions. You can write equivalently:

fit = lm(Ozone ~ Wind + Temp + Wind:Temp, data = airquality)

What is fit here is literally a third predictor that is specified as Wind * Temp (normal multiplication). The above syntax would allow you to also have interactions without main effects, e.g.:

fit = lm(Ozone ~ Wind + Wind:Temp, data = airquality)

Although this is generally never advisable, as the main effect influences the interaction, unless you are sure that the main effect must be zero.
There is another important syntax in R:

fit = lm(Ozone ~ (Wind + Temp + Solar.R)^2 , data = airquality)
summary(fit)


Call:
lm(formula = Ozone ~ (Wind + Temp + Solar.R)^2, data = airquality)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-38.685 -11.727  -2.169   7.360  91.244 

Coefficients:

(Intercept)  -1.408e+02  6.419e+01  -2.193  0.03056 * 
Wind          1.055e+01  4.290e+00   2.460  0.01555 * 
Temp          2.322e+00  8.330e-01   2.788  0.00631 **
Solar.R      -2.260e-01  2.107e-01  -1.073  0.28591   
Wind:Temp    -1.613e-01  5.896e-02  -2.735  0.00733 **
Wind:Solar.R -7.231e-03  6.688e-03  -1.081  0.28212   
Temp:Solar.R  5.061e-03  2.445e-03   2.070  0.04089 * 
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 19.17 on 104 degrees of freedom
  (42 observations deleted due to missingness)
Multiple R-squared:  0.6863,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.6682 
F-statistic: 37.93 on 6 and 104 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16

plot(allEffects(fit), selection = 1)







plot(allEffects(fit), selection = 2)







plot(allEffects(fit), selection = 3)








This creates all main effect and second order (aka two-way) interactions between variables. You can also use ^3 to create all possible 2-way and 3-way interactions between the variables in the parentheses. By the way: The ()^2 syntax for interactions is the reason why we have to write I(x^2) if we want to write a quadratic effect in an lm (see Section 2.5.2).


2.10.2 Interactions with categorical variables
When you include an interaction with a categorical variable, that means a separate effect will be fit for each level of the categorical variable, as in

fit = lm(Ozone ~ Wind * fMonth, data = airquality)
summary(fit)

lm(formula = Ozone ~ Wind * fMonth, data = airquality)

The interpretation is like for a single categorical predictor, i.e. we see the effect of Wind as the effect for the first Month 5, and the Wind:fMonth6 effect, for example, tests for a difference in the Wind effect between month 5 (reference) and month 6. As before, you could change this behavior by changing the contrasts (see the section on contrasts, Section 2.6.1). For example, removing the intercept gives a separate intercept for each month, while the Wind effect is still estimated for month 5, with differences for the other months:

fit = lm(Ozone ~ Wind * fMonth - 1, data = airquality)

and removing also the Wind main effect gives a separate intercept and a separate Wind slope for each month:

fit = lm(Ozone ~ Wind * fMonth - 1 - Wind, data = airquality)



2.10.3 Interactions and centering
A super important topic when working with numeric interactions is centering. To get this started, let’s make a small experiment:






CautionExercise



Compare the estimates for Wind / Temp for the following models

Ozone ~ Wind
Ozone ~ Temp
Ozone ~ Wind + Temp
Ozone ~ Wind * Temp

How do you explain the differences in the estimates for the main effects of Wind and Temp? What do you think corresponds most closely to the “true” effect of Wind and Temp?


What you should have seen in the models above is that the main effects for Wind / Temp change significantly when the interaction is introduced.
Maybe you know the answer already. If not, consider the following simulation, where we create data with known effect sizes:

# Create predictor variables.
x1 = runif(100, -1, 1)
x2 = runif(100, -1, 1)

# Create response for lm, all effects are 1.
y = x1 + x2 + x1*x2 + rnorm(100, sd = 0.3)

# Fit model, but shift the mean of the predictor.
fit = lm(y ~ x1 * I(x2 + 5))
summary(fit)


Call:
lm(formula = y ~ x1 * I(x2 + 5))

Residuals:

-0.78590 -0.24028 -0.01261  0.23085  0.72614 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  -5.52248    0.32056 -17.227  < 2e-16 ***
x1           -3.56776    0.60688  -5.879 5.98e-08 ***
I(x2 + 5)     1.09592    0.06277  17.460  < 2e-16 ***
x1:I(x2 + 5)  0.89799    0.11935   7.524 2.85e-11 ***
---

plot(allEffects(fit))








Play around with the shift in x2, and observe how the effects change. Try how the estimates change when centering the variables via the scale() command. If you understand what’s going on, you will realize that you should always center your variables (Section 2.9.1), whenever you use any interactions.
Excellent explanations of the issues also in Schielzeth (2010).

Schielzeth, H. (2010) “Simple means to improve the interpretability of regression coefficients,” Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 1(2), pp. 103–113. Available at: https://doi.org/10.1111/j.2041-210X.2010.00012.x.
Describing interactions between numeric predictors. With an interaction, the slope of one predictor changes with the value of the other. Instead of interpreting the main effects, you can describe this directly by the slope of one predictor at a few typical values of the other, e.g. its 10%, 50% and 90% quantiles, with confidence intervals. This is easy with the emmeans package (see Section 2.6.3): emtrends() gives the slopes, and emmip() plots the predictions:

library(emmeans)
aq = airquality[complete.cases(airquality[, c("Ozone", "Wind", "Solar.R")]), ]
aq$cWind = aq$Wind - mean(aq$Wind)
aq$cSolar = aq$Solar.R - mean(aq$Solar.R)
fitNN = lm(Ozone ~ cWind * cSolar, data = aq)
q = round(quantile(aq$cSolar, c(0.1, 0.5, 0.9)))
emtrends(fitNN, ~ cSolar, var = "cWind", at = list(cSolar = q))

 cSolar cWind.trend    SE  df lower.CL upper.CL
   -148       -2.34 1.270 107    -4.87    0.184
     22       -5.79 0.667 107    -7.11   -4.465
    100       -7.37 0.960 107    -9.27   -5.468

Confidence level used: 0.95 

emmip(fitNN, cSolar ~ cWind, at = list(cSolar = q, cWind = seq(-7, 10, 1)), CIs = TRUE)








A possible results sentence: “Ozone decreased with wind speed, more strongly at high solar radiation: the slope was -2.3 ppb per mph (95% CI -4.9 to 0.2) at low radiation (10% quantile), -5.8 (-7.1 to -4.5) at median and -7.4 (-9.3 to -5.5) at high radiation (90% quantile).”


2.10.4 Interactions in GAMs
The equivalent of an interaction in a GAM is a tensor spline. It describes how the response varies as a smooth function of 2 predictors. You can specify a tensor spline with the te() command, as in

library(mgcv)
fit = gam(Ozone ~ te(Wind, Temp) , data = airquality)
plot(fit, pages = 0, residuals = T, pch = 20, lwd = 1.9, cex = 0.4)

title: 2  Linear Regression
text:
2.11 Predictions



To predict with a fitted model

fit = lm(Ozone ~ Wind, data = airquality)

we can use the predict() function.

newData = data.frame(Wind = c(5, 10))
predict(fit) # predicts on current data
predict(fit, newdata = newData) # predicts on new data
predict(fit, newdata = newData, se.fit = T)

With se.fit = T, predict() also returns the standard error of the predicted mean. An approximate 95% confidence interval for the mean prediction is fit ± 1.96 * se (large-sample approximation; interval = "confidence" in predict() uses the exact t quantile). For new individual observations use interval = "prediction", which also includes the residual variation and is therefore much wider.
So, let’s predict Ozone with a 95% CI for wind between 2.5 and 10 (within the observed range of 2.3 to 20.7, so that we do not extrapolate):

newData = data.frame(Wind = seq(2.5, 10, 0.1))
pred = predict(fit, newdata = newData, se.fit = T)
lower = pred$fit - 1.96 * pred$se.fit
upper = pred$fit + 1.96 * pred$se.fit
plot(newData$Wind, pred$fit, type = "l", ylim = range(lower, upper), xlab = "Wind", ylab = "Ozone")
lines(newData$Wind, lower, lty = 2)
lines(newData$Wind, upper, lty = 2)

title: 2  Linear Regression
text:
2.12 Nonparametrics and the bootstrap



The linear model (LM) has the beautiful property that it delivers unbiased estimates, calibrated p-values and all that based on analytical expressions that remain valid for any sample size, provided residuals are normally distributed. Unfortunately, there are very few extensions of the LM that completely maintain all of these desirable properties for limited sample sizes. The underlying problem is that for more complicated models, there are usually no closed-form solutions for the expected null or sampling distributions, or those distributions depend on the observed data. For that reason, non-parametric methods to generate confidence intervals and p-values are increasingly used when going to more complicated models, which motivates this first small excursion into non-parametric methods, and in particular cross-validation and the bootstrap.
There are two non-parametric methods that you should absolutely know and that form the backbone of basically all non-parametric for regression analyses with statistical and machine learning models. Those two are:

the bootstrap: generate variance of estimates, allows us to calculate non-parametric CIs and p-values
cross-validation: generate non-parametric estimates of the predictive error of the model (connects to ANOVA and AIC, see the chapters on ANOVA, Chapter 3, and model selection, Chapter 8)

Here, we will look at the bootstrap. Cross-validation will be introduced in the section on cross-validation (Section 8.4).






TipExcursion: randomization null models





Another non-parametric method that you may encounter are randomization null models. Let’s look at this with an example: here, we create data from a normal and a lognormal distribution. We are interested in the difference of the mean of the two (test statistic).

set.seed(1337)

groupA = rnorm(50)
groupB = rlnorm(50)

dat = data.frame(value = c(groupA, groupB), group = factor(rep(c("A", "B"), each = 50)))
plot(value ~ group, data = dat)







# test statistic: difference of the means
reference = mean(groupA) - mean(groupB)

We can show mathematically that the mean of normal draws, standardized by its estimated standard error, follows a Student-t distribution, which is why we can use this distribution in the t-test to calculate the probability of a certain deviation from a null expectation. If we work with different distributions, however, we may not be so sure what the null distribution should be. Either we have to do the (possibly very complicated) math to get a closed-form expression for this problem, or we try to generate a non-parametric expectation for the null distribution via a randomization null model.
The idea is that we generate a null expectation for the test statistic by re-shuffling the data in a way that conforms to the null assumption. In this case, we can just randomize the group labels, which means that we assume that both distributions (A,B) are the same (note that this is a bit more than asking if they have the same mean, but for the sake of the example, we are happy with this simplification).

nSim = 5000
nullDistribution = rep(NA, nSim)

for(i in 1:nSim){
  sel = dat$value[sample.int(100, size = 100)]
  nullDistribution[i] = mean(sel[1:50]) - mean(sel[51:100])
}

hist(nullDistribution, xlim = c(-2,2))
abline(v = reference, col = "red")







(1 + sum(abs(nullDistribution) >= abs(reference))) / (nSim + 1) # two-sided p-value

[1] 0.00019996


Voila, we have a p-value. None of the randomizations was as extreme as the observed difference, so p < 1/nSim; the smallest p-value that we can report is 1/(nSim + 1) (never p = 0), and it is significant. Randomization null models are used in many R packages where analytical p-values are not available, e.g., in the packages vegan (ordinations, community analysis) and bipartite (networks).




2.12.1 Non-parametric bootstrap
The key problem to calculate parametric p-values or CIs is that we need to know the distribution of the statistics of interest that we would obtain if we (hypothetically) repeated the experiment many times. The bootstrap generates new data so that we can approximate this distribution. There are two variants of the bootstrap:

Non-parametric bootstrap: we sample new data from the old data with replacement
Parametric bootstrap: we sample new data from the fitted model

Let’s first look at the non-parametric bootstrap, using a simple regression of Ozone ~ Wind

fit = lm(Ozone ~ Wind, data = airquality)

First, for convenience, we generate a function that extracts the estimate that we want to bootstrap from a fitted model. I decided to extract the slope estimate for Wind, but you could make difference choices

getEstimate <- function(model){
  coef(model)[2]
}
getEstimate(fit)

     Wind 
-5.550923 


Next, we perform the non-parametric bootstrap

performBootstrap = function(){
  sel = sample.int(n = nrow(airquality), replace = T)

  fitNew = lm(Ozone ~ Wind, data = airquality[sel,])
  return(getEstimate(fitNew))
}

bootstrappedEstimate = replicate(1000, performBootstrap())

The bootstrapped estimates of the slope can basically be interpreted as the uncertainty of the slope estimate.

hist(bootstrappedEstimate, breaks = 50)
abline(v = mean(bootstrappedEstimate), col = "red", lwd = 2)
abline(v = getEstimate(fit), col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2)







sd(bootstrappedEstimate)

[1] 0.8314342


We estimate a standard error of 0.83, slightly higher than the parametric error of 0.69 returned by summary.lm()

summary(fit)


Call:
lm(formula = Ozone ~ Wind, data = airquality)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-51.572 -18.854  -4.868  15.234  90.000 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  96.8729     7.2387   13.38  < 2e-16 ***
Wind         -5.5509     0.6904   -8.04 9.27e-13 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 26.47 on 114 degrees of freedom
  (37 observations deleted due to missingness)
Multiple R-squared:  0.3619,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.3563 
F-statistic: 64.64 on 1 and 114 DF,  p-value: 9.272e-13


In R, you don’t have to code the bootstrap by hand, you can also use the boot package. The code will not necessarily be shorter, because you still need to code the statistics, but it offers a few convenient downstream functions for CIs etc.






TipCode for same example using the boot package






# see help, needs arguments d = data, k = index
getBoot = function(d, k){
  fitNew = lm(Ozone ~ Wind, data = d[k,])
  return(getEstimate(fitNew))
}

library(boot)
b1 = boot(airquality, getBoot, R = 1000)
b1


ORDINARY NONPARAMETRIC BOOTSTRAP


Call:
boot(data = airquality, statistic = getBoot, R = 1000)


Bootstrap Statistics :
     original      bias    std. error
t1* -5.550923 -0.04177248   0.8113522







2.12.2 Parametric bootstrap
The parametric bootstrap does the same thing, but the data is not re-sampled, but generated from the fitted model. This can be done conveniently in R as long as the regression package implements a simulate() function that works on the fitted model.

performBootstrapParametric = function(){

  newData = model.frame(fit)
  newData$Ozone = unlist(simulate(fit))

  fitNew = lm(Ozone ~ Wind, data = newData)
  return(getEstimate(fitNew))
}

bootstrappedEstimateParametric = replicate(1000,
                                           performBootstrapParametric())

In the results, we see that the parametric bootstrap is much closer to the analytical results

hist(bootstrappedEstimateParametric, breaks = 50)
abline(v = mean(bootstrappedEstimateParametric), col = "red", lwd = 2)
abline(v = getEstimate(fit), col = "red", lwd = 2, lty = 2)







sd(bootstrappedEstimateParametric)

[1] 0.6835152








TipCode for same example using the boot package





For the parametric bootstrap, we just need a function of the data to return the estimate

getBoot = function(d){
  fitNew = lm(Ozone ~ Wind, data = d)
  return(getEstimate(fitNew))
}

Plus, we need a function that generates the simulations.

rgen = function(dat, mle){
  newData = model.frame(mle)
  newData$Ozone = unlist(simulate(mle))
  return(newData)
}

The call to boot is then

b2 = boot(airquality, getBoot, R = 1000, sim = "parametric", ran.gen = rgen, mle = fit)
b2


PARAMETRIC BOOTSTRAP


Call:
boot(data = airquality, statistic = getBoot, R = 1000, sim = "parametric", 
    ran.gen = rgen, mle = fit)


Bootstrap Statistics :
     original     bias    std. error
t1* -5.550923 0.02205086   0.6735757

title: 2  Linear Regression
text:
2.13 Take-home messages






Tip




Check the residuals before you interpret any p-value or estimate. If the checks reject the model, do not interpret it, change it: first fix a misfit of the mean (functional form), and only then look at distributional problems.
A coefficient in a multiple regression is the effect adjusted for the other predictors in the model. If a collinear predictor is missing, part of its effect is absorbed by the remaining predictors. Collinearity itself does not bias the estimates, but it makes them more uncertain.
For a categorical predictor, the coefficients are differences to the reference level (alphabetically first, change it with relevel()). Test the factor as a whole with an ANOVA, and compare levels with post-hoc tests (e.g. emmeans) that correct for multiple testing.
Center numeric predictors, in particular if the model contains interactions, so that the intercept and main effects refer to a meaningful point in the data. Scaling (by 1 SD) puts effects on a common unit and allows comparing their relative importance, unscaled effects stay interpretable in original units; say which one you report.
Do not conclude “no effect” from a non-significant p-value: say that there is no significant evidence for an effect, and look at the confidence interval to see which effect sizes remain plausible.

2.14 Case studies




2.14.1 Univariate regression






Caution 2.1: Exercise — Plant height



Look at the plantHeight dataset in Ecodata. Let’s assume we want to analyze whether height of plant species from around the world depends on temperature at the location of occurrence. Note that “loght” = log10(height).

library(EcoData)
plot(loght ~ temp, data = plantHeight)









Fit a linear model for this relationship. Perform residual checks (Section 2.4) and modify the model if you think it is necessary (Section 2.5). Interpret the fitted model - how would you present the results in a scientific publication?
The data set also includes a categorical variable “growthform”. Test if growthform has an effect on the plant height. Also, consider changing the reference level of the treatment contrasts (Section 2.6.1) in this case.

Heteroskedasticity - see the chapter on dispersion models (Chapter 10)

title: 3  ANOVA and other tests on the LM
text:
3.1 The idea of ANOVA
ANOVA stands for ANalysis Of VAriance. The basic idea is to find out how much of the signal (variance) is explained by different factors. We had already briefly introduced ANOVA in the section on ANOVA (Section 2.6.2) in the chapter on linear regression.
The problem with explaining ANOVA is that the term is fraught with historical meanings and explanations that are no longer relevant. It used to be that ANOVA is a stand-alone method that you use for experimental designs with different treatments, that ANOVA assumes normal distribution and partitions sum of squares, that there are repeated-measure ANOVAs and all that, and those varieties of ANOVA partly still exist, but in general, there is a much simpler and general explanation of ANOVA:
Modern explanation: ANOVA is not a statistical model, but a hypothesis test that can be performed on top of any regression model. What this test is doing is to measure how much model fit improves when a predictor is added, and if this improvement is significant.
crumbs: 3  ANOVA and other tests on the LM

title: 3  ANOVA and other tests on the LM
text:
3.1.1 An example
As an example, here is an ANOVA (function anova()) performed on the fit of a linear model

fit = lm(Ozone ~ Wind + Temp, data = airquality)
anova(fit)

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: Ozone
           Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
Wind        1  45284   45284  94.808 < 2.2e-16 ***
Temp        1  25886   25886  54.196 3.149e-11 ***
Residuals 113  53973     478                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1




anova() or summary(aov())? For a linear model, anova(fit) and summary(aov(fit)) give the same sequential (type I) ANOVA table. We use anova(), the general R function for comparing models (its use for GLMs and mixed models is discussed in the respective chapters); aov() is mainly needed as input for post-hoc tests such as TukeyHSD() (see Section 2.6.3).
In the standard ANOVA for the LM, model fit is measured by the reduction in residual sum of squares. Let’s look at the example above. In the ANOVA table above, we (virtually) start with an intercept only model. Now, what the table tells us is that adding Wind to the model reduces the Sum Sq. by 45284, and adding also Temp reduces the Sum Sq by another 25886, which leaves us with 53973 residual sum sq. From this, we can also conclude that the total sum of squares of the response is 53973 + 25886 + 45284 = 125143. Let’s check this:

sum((fit$model$Ozone - mean(fit$model$Ozone))^2)

[1] 125143.1


Thus, we can compute the fraction of variance attributed to each model component and to the residuals (note the last entry is the unexplained remainder, not an explained component):

totalSumSq = 45284 + 25886 + 53973 # total sum of squares
45284/totalSumSq # R2 Wind

[1] 0.361858

25886/totalSumSq # R2 Temp

[1] 0.2068514

53973/totalSumSq # unexplained fraction (residual)

[1] 0.4312906


Moreover, the ANOVA table performs tests to see if the improvement of model fit is significant, compared to the model without the respective term. This is important because adding a predictor always improves model fit, even if it has no effect (we will discuss this in more detail in the chapter on model selection, in particular Section 8.2.1).
To interpret the p-values, consider that H0 = the simpler model is true, thus we test if the improvement of model fit is higher than what we would expect if the predictor has no effect.


3.1.2 Customizing the partitioning
An important thing to note is that in an ANOVA, you don’t need to always separate one predictor after the other, you can also work in blocks of predictors, or entire components of the model.
There are a number of cases where this makes a lot of sense. A typical example is, if you are fitting a polynomial of a predictor. Consider, for example, the following regression:

fit = lm(Ozone ~ Wind + I(Wind^2) + Temp + I(Temp^2), data = airquality)

Maybe, we would like to ask how much variance is explained by Wind + Wind^2, and how much by Temp + Temp^2. In this case, we can perform custom ANOVA, using the anova() function that you may have seen in the solution of the exercise in Section 2.5.2, to compare models via a likelihood ratio test (LRT).

m0 = lm(Ozone ~ 1, data = airquality)
m1 = lm(Ozone ~ Wind + I(Wind^2) , data = airquality)
m2 = lm(Ozone ~ Wind + I(Wind^2) + Temp + I(Temp^2), data = airquality)
anova(m0, m1, m2)

Analysis of Variance Table

Model 1: Ozone ~ 1
Model 2: Ozone ~ Wind + I(Wind^2)
Model 3: Ozone ~ Wind + I(Wind^2) + Temp + I(Temp^2)
  Res.Df    RSS Df Sum of Sq      F    Pr(>F)    
1    115 125143                                  
2    113  64360  2     60783 81.397 < 2.2e-16 ***
3    111  41445  2     22915 30.686 2.464e-11 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Which separates the R2 between Wind and Temp, but not between the linear and quadratic effects of the two.

title: 3  ANOVA and other tests on the LM
text:
3.2 Fundamental issues in ANOVA



There are five basic problems that we will come back again when generalizing this principle across a range of models:

How should we measure “improvement of model fit”. Traditionally, improvement is measured by the reduction of the residual sum of squares, but for GLMs, we will have to expand this definition
How should we test if the improvement in fit is significant? For simple models, this is not so much a problem
How should we partition variance if predictors are collinear, and thus the order in which predictors are included matters
Related to the previous point, for categorical predictors, the choice of contrasts changes the results of the type III ANOVA (see Section 3.2.4).
Should we correct for complexity?

Let’s look at the problem one by one:

3.2.1 Measuring model fit
The definition of model fit via sum of squares makes sense as long as we work with linear models.
For GLMs, this definition doesn’t make sense any more. A number of so-called pseudo-R2 metrics have been proposed. Most of them are based on the likelihood (as a measure of model fit) and try to recover as far as possible the properties of an R2 for the linear model.
A common metric is McFadden pseudo-R2, which is defined as 1-[LogL(M)/LogL(M0)], where M is our model, and M0 is an intercept only model. However, many other definitions of “importance” are possible, and in the broadest sense, you could say the principle of ANOVA is to separate out the importance of different predictors or model components, however this importance is measured.


3.2.2 Testing if the improvement is significant
The test used in our example before is an F-test. The F-test is used for models that assume normal distribution. The F-test can be interpreted as a special case of a likelihood ratio test (LRT, for the reason see Tip 3.1), which you may have seen in the solution of the exercise in Section 2.5.2; more on LRTs in the section on likelihood-ratio tests (Section 8.2.1). An LRT compares two nested models, M0 (simpler) and M1:

H0: M0 is true
Test statistic: \(-2 \log \frac{L(M_0)}{L(M_1)} = -2 \left[\log L(M_0) - \log L(M_1)\right]\), i.e. minus twice the difference in maximized log-likelihoods
Under H0 and relatively broad regularity conditions, the test statistic is asymptotically chi-squared distributed, with df = difference in the number of free parameters of the models M1, M0







Tip 3.1: Why the F-test is a likelihood ratio test





The general principle behind both tests is the likelihood ratio test, explained in the section on likelihood-ratio tests (Section 8.2.1). For a linear model with normal residuals, the maximized log-likelihood depends on the data only through the residual sum of squares, \(\log L = -\frac{n}{2} \log(RSS/n) + \text{const}\). The LRT statistic for two nested models is therefore
\[-2 \log \frac{L(M_0)}{L(M_1)} = n \log \frac{RSS_0}{RSS_1} = n \log \left(1 + \frac{q \, F}{n - p_1}\right) \quad \text{with} \quad F = \frac{(RSS_0 - RSS_1)/q}{RSS_1/(n - p_1)},\]
where \(q\) is the number of additional parameters in M1 and \(p_1\) the number of regression coefficients of M1. The LRT statistic is a monotone function of F, so both tests rank all possible results in the same way: the F-test is an LRT. They differ only in the reference distribution. The chi-squared distribution of the LRT is a large-sample approximation, while the F distribution is exact for linear models with normal residuals, because it accounts for the fact that the residual variance is estimated. This is why anova() uses the F-test for lm, and the chi-squared LRT for GLMs and mixed models, for which no exact distribution exists. For nonlinear least squares (Chapter 5), anova() also reports an F-test, but there both distributions are approximations.

datCC = airquality[complete.cases(airquality), ]
mF0 = lm(Ozone ~ Temp, data = datCC)
mF1 = lm(Ozone ~ Temp + Wind, data = datCC)
anova(mF0, mF1) # F-test

Analysis of Variance Table

Model 1: Ozone ~ Temp
Model 2: Ozone ~ Temp + Wind
  Res.Df   RSS Df Sum of Sq      F    Pr(>F)    
1    109 62367                                  
2    108 50989  1     11378 24.101 3.262e-06 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

LR = as.numeric(2 * (logLik(mF1) - logLik(mF0)))
LR # identical to nrow(datCC) * log(1 + F / (nrow(datCC) - 3))

[1] 22.35919

pchisq(LR, df = 1, lower.tail = FALSE) # LRT with chi-squared approximation

[1] 2.261289e-06


With 111 observations, both p-values are practically the same; for small samples, the F-test is the one to use.



This setup works for LMs and GLMs, but runs into problems when the definition how many df a model has is unclear. This is in particular the case for mixed models. In this case, one can resort to simulated LRTs. Simulated LRTs are a special case of the bootstrap (see the section on nonparametrics and the bootstrap, Section 2.12, in particular Section 2.12.2). More precisely, they are a parametric bootstrap: instead of assuming that the test statistic follows a chi-squared distribution (point 3 above), we generate its distribution under H0 by simulating new data from the fitted model M0. Because this method is crucial for mixed models, I want to shortly explain it already here:

Simulate data from H0 (= the fitted model M0)
Re-fit M0 and M1, and calculate likelihood ratios
Repeat n times to get an idea about the expected increase in likelihood when moving to M1 under the assumption that M0 is correct


library(DHARMa)
m0 = lm(Ozone ~ Wind , data = airquality)
m1 = lm(Ozone ~ Wind + Temp, data = airquality)
simulateLRT(m0, m1)









    DHARMa simulated LRT

data:  m0: m0 m1: m1
LogL(M1/M0) = 22.723, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: M1 describes the data better than M0

# for comparison
anova(m0, m1)

Analysis of Variance Table

Model 1: Ozone ~ Wind
Model 2: Ozone ~ Wind + Temp
  Res.Df   RSS Df Sum of Sq      F    Pr(>F)    
1    114 79859                                  
2    113 53973  1     25886 54.196 3.149e-11 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


A simulated p-value cannot be smaller than about 1/(n+1), where n is the number of simulations (250 by default in simulateLRT(), i.e. about 0.004). If none of the simulations reaches the observed value, report p < 1/(n+1) rather than the p-value printed by the function.


3.2.3 Collinearity means that order matters
Another key problem in ANOVA, and a source of much confusion, is how to deal with the fact that often, the order in which model components are added matters. Compare the results of our previous ANOVA with this one, where I only flipped the order of Temp and Wind:

m1 = lm(Ozone ~ Wind + Temp, data = airquality)
m2 = lm(Ozone ~ Temp + Wind, data = airquality)
anova(m1)

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: Ozone
           Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
Wind        1  45284   45284  94.808 < 2.2e-16 ***
Temp        1  25886   25886  54.196 3.149e-11 ***
Residuals 113  53973     478                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

anova(m2)

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: Ozone
           Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
Temp        1  61033   61033 127.781 < 2.2e-16 ***
Wind        1  10137   10137  21.223  1.08e-05 ***
Residuals 113  53973     478                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


The result is markedly different, and the reason is that anova() (like aov()) performs a so-called type I ANOVA. The type I ANOVA adds variables in the order in which they are in the model formula, and because Temp and Wind are collinear, the variable that is added first to the model will absorb variation from the other, and thus seems to explain more of the response.
There are other types of ANOVA that avoid this problem. The so-called type II ANOVA shows for each variable only the part that is uniquely attributable to the respective variable. This is done by discarding the R2 part that is shared by the two predictors due to collinearity (see Figure 3.1 below)

car::Anova(m1, type = "II")

Anova Table (Type II tests)

Response: Ozone
          Sum Sq  Df F value    Pr(>F)    
Wind       10137   1  21.223 1.080e-05 ***
Temp       25886   1  54.196 3.149e-11 ***
Residuals  53973 113                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


There is also type III ANOVA, which, unlike type II, adjusts each term for all other terms, including the interactions it is part of. For such terms, the results depend on centering and contrast coding (details in Caution 3.1 and Section 3.2.4).

car::Anova(m1, type = "III")

Anova Table (Type III tests)

Response: Ozone
            Sum Sq  Df F value    Pr(>F)    
(Intercept)   4335   1  9.0763  0.003196 ** 
Wind         10137   1 21.2230 1.080e-05 ***
Temp         25886   1 54.1960 3.149e-11 ***
Residuals    53973 113                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1




Why is there an (Intercept) row in type III, but not in type II? Type II respects the hierarchy of the model (marginality principle): a term is only tested in models without the terms that build on it, e.g. a main effect A is tested without the interaction A:B. As all terms build on the intercept, the intercept is never tested. Type III, by design, does not follow this hierarchy and tests every term given all others: for the intercept, whether the prediction is zero at Wind = 0 and Temp = 0 (rarely of interest), and for main effects in models with interactions, a hypothesis that depends on centering and coding.
In this model without interaction, type III is identical to type II. Differences only arise for terms that are part of an interaction, as shown in Caution 3.1.






Caution 3.1: Type III ANOVA and centering of numeric predictors



In a model with an interaction x1 * x2, the main effect of x1 describes the effect of x1 at x2 = 0 (see Section 3.2.4.2, Section 2.10.3 and Schielzeth (2010)). The type III ANOVA tests exactly this. If x2 is uncentered, x2 = 0 may be far outside the data (e.g. Wind = 0 mph), and the type III test of x1 then asks a question you are probably not interested in. Centering x2 moves this point to the mean of x2. Type II, in contrast, is not affected by centering:

fit = lm(Ozone ~ scale(Temp) * scale(Wind), data = airquality)
fit2 = lm(Ozone ~ Temp * Wind, data = airquality)

car::Anova(fit, type = "II")

Anova Table (Type II tests)

Response: Ozone
                        Sum Sq  Df F value    Pr(>F)    
scale(Temp)              25886   1  61.966 2.421e-12 ***
scale(Wind)              10137   1  24.266 2.921e-06 ***
scale(Temp):scale(Wind)   7186   1  17.201 6.569e-05 ***

In short: if you run a type III ANOVA on a model with interactions, center all numeric predictors that are part of an interaction, so that main effects are tested at a sensible point (instead of the mean, you can also subtract another value that is meaningful for your question, e.g. a reference temperature; for strongly skewed predictors, the mean may be an atypical value, and the median or a biologically meaningful value is often better). Alternatively, use emmeans::joint_tests(), which needs no centering (see Note 3.1); for the general recommendations, see Section 3.2.3.2.
Polynomial terms are a special case: in x + I(x^2), R does not know that I(x^2) builds on x, so type II and type III both test the linear term at x = 0, and both change with centering. It is usually better to test the polynomial as a whole, e.g. with poly(x, 2) (one test with 2 df), or by comparing models as in Section 3.1.2. poly() builds orthogonal polynomial terms whose coefficients are not directly interpretable, so use it for testing, and x + I(x^2) if you want to interpret the coefficients.
For categorical predictors, the same problem arises through the choice of contrasts. This is explained in Section 3.2.4.
