3.2.3.1 Visualization of ANOVA fractions
Figure 3.1 gives an overview of the situation for 2 predictors A and B and their interaction. The upper left figure corresponds to the case where we have no collinearity between either of those variables. The figure on the top right (and similarly types I - III) are the three possible types of ANOVA for variables with collinearity. The “overlap” between the circles depicts the shared part, i.e. the variability that can be expressed by either variable (due to collinearity). Note that the shares in Type II, III do not add up to 1, as there is a kind of “dark variation” that we cannot securely add to either variable. Take the figure as a heuristic: it describes types I and II well, but type III sums of squares are not a partition of variance at all (the “overlaps” can even be negative). Type III is better understood as testing a particular hypothesis, as explained in Section 3.2.4.2.








Figure 3.1: Heuristic view of how type I, II and III ANOVA assign shared variation between predictors A, B and their interaction (A*B in the figure, A:B in R notation). The type III panel holds only approximately, for sum-to-zero coding and centered predictors.







3.2.3.2 General recommendations
Which type of ANOVA is most appropriate? Unfortunately, the answer is both “it depends on what you want to know” and “there is a lot of discussion about this topic”. I would say the following:

If you have an orthogonal, balanced design, type I and II are identical. Type III is identical as well but ONLY if categorical predictors use sum-to-zero contrasts (see Tip 2.1) and numeric predictors that are part of interactions or polynomial terms are centered (see Section 3.2.4.2).
If not, choose type II or type III ANOVA. Type I is really only appropriate in this case if you explicitly want to have the order-dependence (e.g. if you assume that one of the predictors always takes precedence for biological reasons).
To decide between II and III, note that type II can be read as a (partial) partition of the explained variance, at least in models without interactions, whereas type III sums of squares are better understood as tests of specific hypotheses (main effects at the reference level or the mean of the other predictors). The main question is how main effects should be tested when the model also contains an interaction. We look at this in detail for categorical predictors in Section 3.2.4. Decide before looking at the results, from your question and design, whether the model contains the interaction and whether you are interested in average or in conditional effects, and report the full model either way. Some general hints:

No interaction in the model: use type II (car::Anova(fit)). Without interactions, type II and III are identical anyway. Test polynomial terms as a whole, e.g. with poly(x, 2) (see Caution 3.1).
Interaction in the model: a main effect is now an average over an effect that varies, so ask yourself first if such an average is meaningful for your question. Often, it is more informative to describe the interaction directly, i.e. the effect of one predictor at different values of the other (simple effects; for numeric predictors, see Section 2.10.3; for factors, see Note 3.1). Judge the interaction by its estimated simple effects with confidence intervals, not by its p-value; if they differ strongly, point out that a main effect is only an average over them. If you do want main effects, both types are defensible:

Type II (the default of car::Anova()) tests main effects without the interaction, i.e. respecting the hierarchy of the model (marginality principle, Nelder, 1977). Variance shared between main effects and interaction stays with the main effects, so if the interaction is weak, type II is often the more powerful test. With a substantial interaction, however, the main effect is an average over the other predictor whose weights depend on the cell sizes (but are not simply proportional to them).
Type III tests main effects averaged with equal weights over the other predictor, a hypothesis that is independent of the design and remains meaningful if there is an interaction; if the interaction is in fact weak, it has somewhat less power than type II. It requires centered numeric predictors (Caution 3.1) and, for factors, sum-to-zero contrasts (Section 3.2.4).
Which of the two is preferable is debated (e.g. Shaw and Mitchell-Olds (1993) favour type III, Langsrud (2003) and Fox and Weisberg (2019) type II; see also Hector, Von Felten and Schmid (2010)); report which one you used. The test of the interaction itself is identical in both. Don’t remove an interaction only because it is not significant to simplify the ANOVA; this is a model selection step (see the chapter on model selection, in particular Section 8.3).


Note that for reasonably balanced and orthogonal data, as they occur in controlled experiments, type II and type III with sum-to-zero contrasts usually give nearly identical results. However, with stronger imbalance or collinearity together with an interaction, differences tend to get larger, even with correct coding and centering (type II then often, but not always, gives the larger F values), and partitioning can get fragile due to the large shared components. Such differences are not a sign of an error, but reflect that the two types test different hypotheses (see the example in Hector, Von Felten and Schmid, 2010). Note that collinearity is not restricted to numeric predictors: a factor can also be correlated with a numeric predictor (e.g. if some islands lie at higher elevations than others), with the same consequences for the order dependence of type I and the differences between type II and III. Check collinearity, e.g. with the correlation between predictors or, with more predictors, with variance inflation factors of the model without interactions (see Section 2.8; with interaction terms, vif() warns and the values are not meaningful), and center the predictors. Type II is robust to centering and coding, but a main effect is only interpretable as such if the interaction is weak; type III can differ considerably, in particular when predictors are skewed, correlated and interact. Don’t read a loss of significance as the loss of an effect, or shared fractions as causal importance, and put more emphasis on effect estimates with confidence intervals, on testing blocks of predictors by model comparison (Section 3.1.2), or on hierarchical partitioning (Lai, Zou, J. Zhang, et al., 2022; Lai, Zou, S. Zhang, et al., 2022).
Note also that, for many cases, there are good alternatives to ANOVA. ANOVA derives its popularity from its long history for balanced experimental designs, and its presence in every textbook. For unbalanced collinear observation data, however, standardized effect sizes, average marginal effects or marginal means (see Note 3.1) may be better choices.

3.2.4 Categorical predictors: contrasts influence ANOVA results
For categorical predictors, a complication occurs that is related, but not identical, to the issues discussed in Section 3.2.3: in case of collinearity, type I, II and III ANOVA can give very different answers (as before), but type III additionally depends on how the factors’ contrasts are coded (see Section 2.6.1). As this regularly causes confusion, let’s look at a typical example.

3.2.4.1 The problem
Imagine a field experiment with three fertilizer treatments (control, N, NP), crossed with grazing (plots fenced or open to grazers). The design was planned balanced, but some plots were lost, so the number of plots per treatment combination now differs:

set.seed(1)
plots = expand.grid(fertilizer = c("control", "N", "NP"),
                    grazing = c("fenced", "open"))
plots$n = c(12, 5, 9, 4, 15, 7)     # remaining plots per combination
plots$mu = c(0, 1, 2, 0.5, 1.5, 4)  # true treatment effects
plots = plots[rep(1:6, plots$n), ]
plots$biomass = rnorm(nrow(plots), mean = 5 + plots$mu)

table(plots$fertilizer, plots$grazing)

         
          fenced open
  control     12    4
  N            5   15
  NP           9    7


Before fitting, it is always worth checking the order of the factor levels, because the first level is the reference level for R’s default treatment contrasts. Factors created from character vectors (e.g. by factor(), or when reading data) are ordered alphabetically, and whether upper or lower case comes first can depend on your computer settings. Here, expand.grid() keeps the order we gave, so control is the first level and thus the reference, as we want:

levels(plots$fertilizer)

[1] "control" "N"       "NP"     

# plots$fertilizer = relevel(plots$fertilizer, ref = "control") # if needed

relevel() only changes the reference level. To set the order of all levels, e.g. for a treatment none / low / high (which R would sort as high, low, none), use factor(x, levels = c("none", "low", "high")).
Because the design is unbalanced, fertilizer and grazing are no longer independent (orthogonal): e.g. most N plots are open. As a consequence, the type I ANOVA depends on the order of the predictors. Grazing gets F = 18.9 when it is added first, but F = 14.2 when it is added after fertilizer:

3.2.4.2 What is going on?
The key to understanding this is the following:
The coding of a factor never changes the fitted model. It only changes which hypotheses the individual coefficients and the type III tests examine.
We can confirm the first part of the statement by looking at the predictions of the two models, which are indeed identical:

all.equal(fitted(fit), fitted(fitSum))

[1] TRUE




This holds as long as the model contains all lower-order terms of each interaction. If you, e.g., remove a main effect but keep its interaction, or use uncorrelated random slopes in a mixed model (see Caution 4.2), the coding also changes the model itself.
For the second part, we have to consider what hypothesis / comparisons are expressed by the contrasts. In a model with interactions, every lower-order term (a main effect, or a two-way interaction in a model with a three-way interaction) is estimated and tested at the zero point of the variables it interacts with. This zero point is

for a treatment-coded factor (R default): the reference level
for a sum-to-zero coded factor (contr.sum, contr.helmert, contr.poly; see Tip 2.1): the unweighted average over its levels
for a numeric predictor: the value 0, or the centering value if the predictor was centered

Thus, with treatment contrasts, the “main effect” of grazing in the type III ANOVA is the effect of grazing in the control plots (the reference level of fertilizer), where grazing has hardly any effect. With sum-to-zero contrasts, it is the effect of grazing averaged equally over the three fertilizer treatments. Both tests are correct, they just answer different questions. Note that this is the same rule that you already know from the regression table: in summary(fit), the grazing estimate is the effect of grazing at the reference level of fertilizer. The same applies to the (Intercept) row of the type III table: with treatment contrasts, it tests if the mean of fenced control plots is zero, with sum-to-zero contrasts if the unweighted average over all treatment combinations is zero.

Thus, if you want type III tests of main effects that are averaged over the levels of the other factors, use sum-to-zero contrasts for all factors, and center all numeric predictors that are part of an interaction. Centering means subtracting the mean (or another meaningful value), e.g. dat$cx = dat$x - mean(dat$x) (see Section 2.10.3). Set the contrasts locally in the model call via contrasts = list(...), as we did for fitSum above.
You can also change contrasts globally via options(contrasts = c("contr.sum", "contr.poly")), but this silently changes the meaning of all coefficients in every model you fit afterwards (reset with options(contrasts = c("contr.treatment", "contr.poly"))). Note also that the coefficients of a sum-coded model (grazing1, fertilizer1, …) in summary() are deviations from the average over levels and are hard to read. Don’t report them, report estimated means instead (see Note 3.1).
What about type II? Type II (the default of car::Anova()) does not depend on the coding (grazing: F = 14.2, p = 0.0005), but in a model with an interaction, it tests grazing while ignoring the interaction. Roughly speaking, it averages the grazing effect over the fertilizer treatments with weights that depend on the number of plots per combination (but are not simply proportional to it). If the interaction is weak, this is the more powerful test; if it is strong, the result is harder to interpret. Whether type II or type III is preferable in such cases is debated; Section 3.2.3.2 and Section 3.2.4.3 give pragmatic recommendations. Here is the type II ANOVA for our example:

If the interaction matters, the effect of one factor at each level of the other (simple effects) is usually more informative than any main effect. Such simple effects, as well as comparisons between individual treatments, are best calculated with the emmeans package:






Note 3.1: The emmeans package





emmeans is not an ANOVA, but a general tool to interpret fitted models (lm, glm and mixed models), based on three ideas:

Estimated marginal means: predicted means for each factor level or combination of levels, averaged over the other factors, with numeric predictors at their mean (unless specified otherwise). As model predictions, they don’t depend on how factors are coded.
Equal weights: by default, all levels that are averaged over get the same weight, which corresponds to the main-effect hypotheses of a type III ANOVA with sum-to-zero contrasts (for alternatives, see below).
Adjusted comparisons: differences between these means are tested as contrasts, adjusted for multiple testing, e.g. Tukey for all pairs, or Dunnett for comparisons against a control.

 N - control     1.512 0.467 46   3.240  0.0043
 NP - control    4.062 0.520 46   7.815 <0.0001

P value adjustment: dunnettx method for 2 tests 

plot(emm)








Simple effects are not an interaction. At first sight, N seems to increase biomass only on open plots (+1.51, p = 0.004), but not on fenced plots (+0.38, p = 0.60, only 5 plots). But “significant in one group, not significant in the other” is not evidence for an interaction: the difference between significant and not significant is not itself significant (Gelman and Stern, 2006); whether the N effect differs between grazing treatments has to be tested directly:

contrast(emmeans(fit, ~ fertilizer * grazing),
         interaction = c("trt.vs.ctrl", "pairwise"), ref = "control")

 fertilizer_trt.vs.ctrl grazing_pairwise estimate    SE df t.ratio p.value
 N - control            fenced - open       -1.14 0.642 46  -1.767  0.0838
 NP - control           fenced - open       -2.03 0.635 46  -3.194  0.0025


Each row is a difference of differences: the effect of a fertilizer compared to the control (trt.vs.ctrl) within each grazing treatment, compared between the treatments (pairwise, i.e. fenced minus open; p-values not adjusted for multiple testing). The N effect is 1.14 larger on open plots, but this difference is not significant (p = 0.084): we cannot claim an interaction for N, although this does not prove that the N effects are equal. Indeed, the data were simulated with the same true N effect (+1) in both treatments. The interaction is driven by NP (difference 2.03, p = 0.0025; simulated true effects +2 on fenced and +3.5 on open plots), which is arguably more informative than any main effect.
F-tests. joint_tests() combines these comparisons into F-tests per model term; with by, separately for fenced and open plots:

joint_tests(fit, by = "grazing")

grazing = fenced:
 model term df1 df2 F.ratio p.value
 fertilizer   2  46  16.165 <0.0001

grazing = open:
 model term df1 df2 F.ratio p.value
 fertilizer   2  46  35.851 <0.0001


Without by, joint_tests() gives exactly the type III ANOVA with sum-to-zero contrasts and numeric predictors at their mean, regardless of how the model was coded, i.e. without recoding or centering (see Section 3.2.4.2 and Caution 3.1; for type II, use car::Anova(fit) instead):

joint_tests(fit)

 model term         df1 df2 F.ratio p.value
 grazing              1  46  11.456  0.0015
 fertilizer           2  46  50.350 <0.0001
 grazing:fertilizer   2  46   5.100  0.0100


Main effects in models with interaction. Means of one factor only, e.g. emmeans(fit, ~ grazing), are averaged over the other factor. The note “Results may be misleading due to involvement in interactions” is not an error, but a reminder that the grazing effect differs between fertilizer treatments.
Unequal weights. Equal weights suit designed experiments where group sizes differ by accident, as in our experiment with lost plots. In observational data, group sizes often reflect the population (e.g. a common vs. a rare habitat type), and equal weights then describe a balanced population that may not exist. To average proportional to group sizes, use weights = "proportional" (this only matters if you average over another factor):

emm = emmeans(fit, ~ grazing, weights = "proportional")
pairs(emm)

Factor × numeric interactions. emtrends() gives the slope of the numeric predictor for each factor level, and the at argument sets the value of the numeric predictor at which the levels are compared:

airquality$fMonth = factor(airquality$Month)
fitAQ = lm(Ozone ~ Temp * fMonth, data = airquality)
emtrends(fitAQ, ~ fMonth, var = "Temp")         # Temp slope per month

Confidence level used: 0.95 

emmeans(fitAQ, ~ fMonth, at = list(Temp = 80))  # months compared at 80 °F

NOTE: Results may be misleading due to involvement in interactions


 fMonth emmean    SE  df lower.CL upper.CL

Confidence level used: 0.95 


Choose this value deliberately, and within the observed range of each group (tapply(airquality$Temp, airquality$fMonth, range)); otherwise you extrapolate.
Interactions between numeric predictors. How to describe an interaction between two numeric predictors with emtrends() is shown in the section on interactions and centering (Section 2.10.3).
Empty cells. If a treatment combination has no data at all, car::Anova(type = "III") stops with “there are aliased coefficients in the model”, while type II and joint_tests() run without an error, but test hypotheses that are hard to interpret (look for reduced df, or for “(confounded)” in the output of joint_tests()). One option is to fit one mean per existing combination and to test the comparisons you are interested in with custom contrasts, here after removing the fenced N plots:

plots2 = plots[!(plots$fertilizer == "N" & plots$grazing == "fenced"), ]
plots2$combination = interaction(plots2$fertilizer, plots2$grazing, drop = TRUE)
levels(plots2$combination)

[1] "control.fenced" "NP.fenced"      "control.open"   "N.open"        
[5] "NP.open"       

fitComb = lm(biomass ~ combination, data = plots2)
emm = emmeans(fitComb, ~ combination)
contrast(emm, list(NP_vs_control_fenced = c(-1, 1, 0, 0, 0),
                   NP_vs_control_open   = c(0, 0, -1, 0, 1)))

 contrast             estimate    SE df t.ratio p.value
 NP_vs_control_fenced     2.03 0.345 42   5.892 <0.0001
 NP_vs_control_open       4.06 0.490 42   8.285 <0.0001


The weights in the list refer to the levels in the order printed by levels(). Simply dropping the interaction instead assumes that the effects of the two factors add up.
Reporting emmeans results. Report the estimated means or differences with their CIs (ideally as a plot, e.g. plot(emm)), which comparisons you made and how p-values were adjusted (e.g. “Dunnett-adjusted contrasts against the control, calculated with the emmeans package”), and, if you averaged over other factors, whether with equal or proportional weights.




Gelman, A. and Stern, H. (2006) “The difference between ‘significant’ and ‘not significant’ is not itself statistically significant,” The American Statistician, 60(4), pp. 328–331. Available at: https://doi.org/10.1198/000313006X152649.


3.2.4.3 Practical recommendations for categorical predictors
The general recommendations in Section 3.2.3.2 also apply to categorical predictors. In addition, note the following:

Reference level and contrasts: check the order of the factor levels before fitting, and set the reference level deliberately (see Section 3.2.4.1). With R’s default treatment contrasts, it determines what the coefficients in summary() refer to, and also what type III main-effect tests refer to. For a type III ANOVA, therefore set sum-to-zero contrasts locally, e.g. contrasts = list(fertilizer = contr.sum, grazing = contr.sum), and never interpret a type III ANOVA with treatment contrasts as main effects.
Interactions between factors: judge them by the estimated differences between simple effects and their confidence intervals. The interaction test alone tells you neither where effects differ nor, if it is not significant, that they are equal. Separate tests within each group are no substitute: “significant in one group, not in the other” is not an interaction.
Unequal group sizes: with sum-to-zero contrasts, type III weights all treatment combinations equally, which suits designed experiments where cell sizes differ by accident. The weights of type II depend on the cell sizes, but are not proportional to them, so type II does not give population-weighted averages either. If you want averages weighted by group sizes, e.g. in observational data where group sizes reflect the population, use emmeans with weights = "proportional" (Note 3.1).
Small and empty cells: report the number of observations per treatment combination (table()), as combinations with very few observations (as a rough rule of thumb, fewer than about 5) give imprecise estimates, which show up as wide confidence intervals; this also makes the difference between type II and III less predictable. If a combination is empty, type III cannot be computed, and type II tests hypotheses that are hard to interpret; dropping the interaction instead assumes that the effects of the two factors add up.

Alternative: estimated marginal means. Many of these questions (simple effects, comparisons between individual treatments, the choice of weights, empty cells) can be answered more directly with the emmeans package, which may be the better choice, as its results do not depend on contrast coding (see Note 3.1).
Reporting. An example for the methods: “Biomass was analyzed with a linear model including fertilizer, grazing and their interaction. We tested effects with type III F-tests based on sum-to-zero contrasts (car::Anova), and compared fertilizer treatments against the control within each grazing treatment with Dunnett-adjusted contrasts (emmeans).” If you use type II, write “type II F-tests (car::Anova)” instead. For how to report estimated means and comparisons, see the end of Note 3.1.
Mixed models: the type III ANOVA of the lmerTest package is an exception, as it does not depend on the coding (see Caution 4.2).






CautionExercise — Does coding matter?

3.2.5 Correcting partitions for complexity
A last problem is that while the calculation of the p-value in the LRT (see Section 3.2.2) corrects for the fact that model components with more complexity (df) will always tend to explain more variance, the naive variance components / R2 that we calculate in the ANOVA are uncorrected for this problem.

Here, we see that the adjusted R2 is considerably lower than the raw R2, even though not zero. For a simple LM and a type I ANOVA, a first-order solution would thus be to re-calculate the R2 components with adjusted values: compute the adjusted R2 for the sequence of nested models, and use the differences between them as components. For example, adding Day to a model with Wind increases the raw R2 by 0.23, but the adjusted R2 only by 0.08, while the adjustment hardly changes the R2 of Wind, which uses only 1 df (0.36 raw and adjusted):

R2 = function(f) summary(lm(f, data = airquality))$r.squared
adjR2 = function(f) summary(lm(f, data = airquality))$adj.r.squared

[1] 0.229653

[1] 0.3562605

[1] 0.08449894


For more complex models in general (mixed models, hierarchical models), reliably adjusting R2 components for complexity in an ANOVA is very complicated. I would recommend that

If you report raw components (which is the default in most papers), consider that this is a description of your model, not an inference about the true variance created by the respective factor, and include in your interpretation that variables or model components with more df will always tend to explain more variance
A possibility is to calculate variance explained via a cross-validation on a hold-out data. If a sensible cross-validation can be set up (which is not trivial if there are cluster / correlation structures in your data), this is a relatively stable metric of variance explained.
Alternatively, you could adjust R2 by a null expectation, similar to the parametric bootstrap for the LRT (Section 3.2.2). However, because you subtract what is expected under H0, this will be a conservative estimate.

3.3 Relationship between lm and other hypotheses tests



ANOVA is just one example of the close relationship between the lm and other null hypothesis significance tests. ANOVA can either be seen as a special test (traditional view), or as a special evaluation of a fitted lm (modern view). I would recommend taking the modern view, as it easily generalizes to GLMs and other more advanced regression models such as GLMMs.
It is interesting to consider more generally which hypothesis tests can be obtained by looking at certain results or tests on the linear model. As you can see in the table below, there are many classical hypothesis tests that are equivalently or nearly equivalently tested by a linear model.

Common statistical tests with linear models







Hypothesis
R function
Equivalent linear model




Two groups differ in their means
unpaired t.test
t.test(y_1, y_2, var.equal = TRUE)
lm(c(y_1, y_2)~c(g_1, g_2))


Two groups differ in their means
paired t.test
t.test(y_1, y_2, paired = TRUE)
lm(y_2-y_1~1)


y depends on continuous x
Pearson correlation
cor.test(x, y)
lm(y~x), identical p-value for the slope


y depends on continuous x
Spearman correlation
cor.test(x, y, method = "spearman")
lm(rank(y)~rank(x)) note: only near-equivalent.


y differs between groups
One-way ANOVA
aov(y~group)
lm(y~group) with subsequent ANOVA



Based on this, one could think it doesn’t matter then if we use a regression model or a hypothesis test. However, the advantage of the regression model is that

It provides a richer output
It provides the same output for all cases, with clear ideas about how to check residuals etc.
It allows us to adjust for the effects of covariates

text:
3.4 Take-home messages






Tip




An ANOVA is not a model but a test that is run on a fitted model: it asks how much the fit improves when a term is added, and whether this improvement is larger than expected if the term had no effect.
With collinear or unbalanced data, the type I ANOVA depends on the order of the terms in the formula. Use type II if the model has no interaction; with interactions, think about which hypothesis you want to test. Report which type you used.
The coding of a factor never changes the fitted model, but it changes type III tests of terms that are part of an interaction. With type III, use sum-to-zero contrasts and center numeric predictors in interactions, or use emmeans::joint_tests(), which does not depend on the coding.
If the model has an interaction, describe the effect of one predictor at the levels (or values) of the other, with estimates and confidence intervals (emmeans). “Significant in one group, not significant in the other” is not evidence for an interaction; test the difference of the effects.
Raw sums of squares and R2 fractions describe your fitted model, are not the true importance of a predictor, and are too high for terms with many df (e.g. a factor with many levels). For a simple lm use the adjusted R2; for more complex models report the raw fractions as a description only, or use cross-validation on hold-out data.

title: 3  ANOVA and other tests on the LM
text:
3.5 Case studies




3.5.1 Plant height
Let’s look at our plant height case study from the chapter on linear regression (see the plant height exercise, Caution 2.2). Which type of ANOVA should you run to analyze the model? Compare results to “less appropriate” alternatives.

library(EcoData)
fit = lm(loght ~ temp * lat, data = plantHeight)
summary(fit)


Call:
lm(formula = loght ~ temp * lat, data = plantHeight)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-1.97905 -0.45112  0.01062  0.42852  1.74054 

Coefficients:
              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept)  2.917e-01  5.617e-01   0.519    0.604
temp         2.596e-02  2.040e-02   1.273    0.205
lat         -8.948e-03  9.711e-03  -0.921    0.358
temp:lat     7.738e-05  3.061e-04   0.253    0.801

Residual standard error: 0.6869 on 174 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.2504,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.2375 
F-statistic: 19.37 on 3 and 174 DF,  p-value: 6.95e-11








TipSolution





This is the case of collinear observational data from Section 3.2.3.2: temperature and latitude are strongly correlated,

cor(plantHeight$temp, plantHeight$lat)

[1] -0.9249304


and the model contains their interaction. We therefore center the predictors, so that type III tests each main effect at the mean of the other predictor (type II is not affected by centering):

plantHeight$stemp = scale(plantHeight$temp, scale = FALSE) # only center variable
plantHeight$slat = scale(plantHeight$lat, scale = FALSE)
fit = lm(loght ~ stemp * slat, data = plantHeight)
summary(fit)


Call:
lm(formula = loght ~ stemp * slat, data = plantHeight)

Residuals:
     Min       1Q   Median       3Q      Max 
-1.97905 -0.45112  0.01062  0.42852  1.74054 

Coefficients:
              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  4.694e-01  6.771e-02   6.932 7.78e-11 ***
stemp        2.838e-02  1.543e-02   1.839   0.0676 .  
slat        -7.700e-03  8.020e-03  -0.960   0.3383    
stemp:slat   7.738e-05  3.061e-04   0.253   0.8007    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 0.6869 on 174 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.2504,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.2375 
F-statistic: 19.37 on 3 and 174 DF,  p-value: 6.95e-11


The type II ANOVA discards shared fractions between main effects. Note that because of the high collinearity, R2 assigned to each predictor is extremely low.

print(car::Anova(fit, type = "II"))

Anova Table (Type II tests)

Response: loght
           Sum Sq  Df F value  Pr(>F)  
stemp       1.888   1  4.0014 0.04702 *
slat        0.421   1  0.8922 0.34620  
stemp:slat  0.030   1  0.0639 0.80074  
Residuals  82.089 174                  
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


The type III ANOVA, unlike type II, also adjusts the main effects for the interaction. Here, this changes the sums of squares of the main effects only slightly (temp somewhat lower, lat essentially unchanged), but temp now just misses the 0.05 threshold. The difference arises only because the model contains the (here clearly non-significant, p = 0.80) interaction: without it, type II and III are identical (temp p = 0.046). With r = -0.92 between temp and lat, even the centered interaction term is correlated with the main effects (r = 0.53 with temp and -0.47 with lat), so adjusting for it, as type III does, changes their tests (Section 3.2.3.2). Both types are defensible, and the difference mainly shows that the data cannot clearly separate the effects of temperature and latitude, so don’t overinterpret the 0.05 threshold.

print(car::Anova(fit, type = "III"))

Anova Table (Type III tests)

Response: loght
            Sum Sq  Df F value    Pr(>F)    
(Intercept) 22.670   1 48.0522 7.782e-11 ***
stemp        1.596   1  3.3834   0.06756 .  
slat         0.435   1  0.9218   0.33834    
stemp:slat   0.030   1  0.0639   0.80074    
Residuals   82.089 174                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Generally, because of its order dependence under collinearity, you should be hesitant to run a type I ANOVA. However, there can be reasons to do it. For example, in this case, you may argue that temperature is a more plausible or mechanistic predictor than latitude. For that reason, you could say that you want to explain everything by temperature first, and then see if latitude can explain something on top of temperature. If that is your goal, you can also run a type I ANOVA.

anova(fit)

Analysis of Variance Table

Response: loght
            Df Sum Sq Mean Sq F value    Pr(>F)    
stemp        1 26.967 26.9669 57.1602 2.211e-12 ***
slat         1  0.421  0.4209  0.8922    0.3462    
stemp:slat   1  0.030  0.0301  0.0639    0.8007    
Residuals  174 82.089  0.4718                      
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


As a last, add-on, let’s see what happens when we use the non centered variables:

fit2 = lm(loght ~ temp * lat, data = plantHeight)
print(car::Anova(fit2, type = "II"))

Anova Table (Type II tests)

Response: loght
          Sum Sq  Df F value  Pr(>F)  
temp       1.888   1  4.0014 0.04702 *
lat        0.421   1  0.8922 0.34620  
temp:lat   0.030   1  0.0639 0.80074  
Residuals 82.089 174                  
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

print(car::Anova(fit2, type = "III"))

Anova Table (Type III tests)

Response: loght
            Sum Sq  Df F value Pr(>F)
(Intercept)  0.127   1  0.2696 0.6043
temp         0.764   1  1.6198 0.2048
lat          0.401   1  0.8490 0.3581
temp:lat     0.030   1  0.0639 0.8007
Residuals   82.089 174               


Type II is unchanged, but type III changes: the main effect of temp is now tested at lat = 0 (the equator) and vice versa, which is a different and, for this dataset, rather meaningless hypothesis. This is an example of a more general point: if you run type III ANOVAs, center numeric predictors and use sum-to-zero contrasts for factors (or use emmeans::joint_tests(), see Note 3.1).

title: 4  Linear mixed models
text:
4.1 Motivation
Random effects are a very common addition to regression models that are used to account for grouping (categorical) variables such as subject, year, location. To explain the motivation for these models, as well as the basic syntax, we will use an example data set containing exam scores of 4,059 students from 65 schools in Inner London. This data set is located in the R package mlmRev.
If we analyze this with a simple LM, we see that reading ability and sex have the expected effects on the exam score.
library(mlmRev)
library(effects)

mod0 = lm(normexam ~ standLRT + sex , data = Exam)
plot(allEffects(mod0))
However, it is reasonable to assume that not all schools are equally good, which has two possible consequences:
We could solve this problem by fitting a different mean per school
mod0b = lm(normexam ~ standLRT + sex + school , data = Exam)
however, with 65 schools this would cost 64 degrees of freedom, which is a high cost just for correcting the possibility of confounding and a minor residual problem.
The solution: Mixed / random effect models. In a mixed model, we assume (differently to a fixed effect model) that the variance between schools originates from a normal distribution. There are different interpretations of a random effect (more on this in Section 4.3.1), but one interpretation is to view the random effect as an additional error, so that such a mixed model has two levels of error:
Because of this hierarchical structure, these models are also called “multi-level models” or “hierarchical models”.

title: 4  Linear mixed models
text:
Response: “normexam” (Normalized exam score).
Predictor 1: “standLRT” (Standardized LR test score; Reading test taken when they were 11 years old).
Predictor 2: “sex” of the student (F / M).
Grouping factor: school





If school identity correlates with sex or standLRT, school could be a confounder (see Section 4.4.4 for a check, and the chapter on causal inference, Chapter 7)
Residuals will be correlated within schools, thus they are not iid (pseudo-replication)






First, the random effect, which is a normal “error” acting on an entire group of data points (in this case school).
And second, the residual error, which is a normal error per observation and acts on top of the random effect








Note



Because grouping naturally occurs in any type of experimental data (batches, blocks, observer, subject etc.), random and mixed effect models are the de-facto default for most experimental data! Naming conventions:

No random effect = fixed effect model
Only random effects = random effect model
Random effects + fixed effects = mixed model

Most models that are used in practice are mixed models

title: 4  Linear mixed models
text:
4.2 Specifying and estimating mixed models




4.2.1 The random intercept model
The simplest random effect structure is the random intercept model.
Each random effect model has a fixed counterpart. For the random intercept model, this counterpart is the model we already saw in Section 4.1, with school as a fixed effect

mod0b = lm(normexam ~ standLRT + sex + school , data = Exam)

The random intercept model is practically identical to the model above, except that it assumes that the school effects come from a common normal distribution. The model can be estimated with lme4::lmer

library(lme4)
mod1 = lmer(normexam ~ standLRT + sex +  (1 | school), data = Exam)
summary(mod1)

Linear mixed model fit by REML ['lmerMod']
Formula: normexam ~ standLRT + sex + (1 | school)
   Data: Exam

REML criterion at convergence: 9346.6

Scaled residuals: 
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-3.7120 -0.6314  0.0166  0.6855  3.2735 

Random effects:
 Groups   Name        Variance Std.Dev.
 school   (Intercept) 0.08986  0.2998  
 Residual             0.56252  0.7500  
Number of obs: 4059, groups:  school, 65

Fixed effects:
            Estimate Std. Error t value
(Intercept)  0.07639    0.04202   1.818
standLRT     0.55947    0.01245  44.930
sexM        -0.17136    0.03279  -5.226

Correlation of Fixed Effects:
         (Intr) stnLRT
standLRT -0.013       
sexM     -0.337  0.061


If we look at the outputs, you will probably note that the summary() function doesn’t return p-values. More on this in Section 4.5.1. Also, we see that the effects of the individual school are not explicitly mentioned. The summary only returns the mean effects over all schools, and the variance between schools (Random effects block: the school sd of 0.30 compares with the residual sd of 0.75, i.e. school accounts for about 14% of the variance that the fixed effects do not explain, the intraclass correlation). However, you can obtain the individual school effects via

ranef(mod1)

Moreover, unlike the outputs we have seen before, the model also returns a correlation between fixed effect estimates. This, however, is simply a choice of the programmers, it has nothing to do with the random effect models - you could calculate the same output for the lm() via the function vcov().
Here is a visualization of the fitted effects for standLRT









We can see that there is the same slope, but a different intercept per school.
The RE effectively “centers” the categorical predictor - unlike for the fixed effect model, where the intercept would be interpreted as the value for the first school, the intercept in the random effect model is the mean across all schools, and the REs measure the deviation of the individual school from the mean. It should be stressed, however, that this is a welcome consequence, but not the main motivation, for the RE structure.






TipGenerate equation with the equatiomatic package





We can use the equatiomatic package to print LaTeX code for the underlying equation of our random intercept model:

library(equatiomatic)
extract_eq(mod1)

\[\begin{aligned}
  \operatorname{normexam}_{i}  &\sim N \left(\alpha_{j[i]} + \beta_{1}(\operatorname{standLRT}) + \beta_{2}(\operatorname{sex}_{\operatorname{M}}), \sigma^2 \right) \\
    \alpha_{j}  &\sim N \left(\mu_{\alpha_{j}}, \sigma^2_{\alpha_{j}} \right)
    \text{, for school j = 1,} \dots \text{,J}
\end{aligned}\]









Tip 4.1: From study design to random effects



The random effect structure should follow from the design of the study, not from the data. Ask yourself:

What is the experimental unit, i.e. the unit to which a treatment was applied, or at which a predictor varies? If you have several measurements per unit (several plants per plot, several visits per site), these measurements are not independent replicates. Treating them as if they were is called pseudoreplication (Hurlbert, 1984) and makes p-values too small. A random intercept for the unit (here (1|plot)) accounts for this when the treatment varies between units: the effective sample size is then roughly the number of plots, not the number of plants. The same applies to any predictor that is constant within a unit, e.g. the elevation of a site that was surveyed repeatedly.
How are the units grouped? Typical designs and their random effects:

randomized blocks: y ~ treatment + (1|block)
several measurements per plot (subsampling): y ~ treatment + (1|plot)
split-plot (factor A on main plots, factor B on subplots within the main plots): y ~ A * B + (1|block/mainplot) (/ means nested: main plots within blocks, see Tip 4.2)
repeated measurements of the same units over time: y ~ treatment * time + (1|site), possibly with a temporal correlation structure (Section 11.2)
two independent grouping factors, e.g. sites and observers: y ~ x + (1|site) + (1|observer) (crossed random effects, Tip 4.2)

Does the grouping factor have enough levels? The variance of a random effect is estimated from its levels. A common rule of thumb is therefore that a random effect needs at least about 5-10 levels, and that a grouping variable with fewer levels is better modeled as a fixed effect (Bolker, 2015; Harrison et al., 2018). The discussion is, however, nuanced (see Section 4.3.3): with few levels, singular fits (variance estimated as zero) are common, but simulations suggest that the tests of the population-level effects can still be reliable (Oberpriller, Souza Leite and Pichler, 2022).
Is there structure left after that? Correlation within units over time (Section 11.2) or changing variance (Chapter 10) can be modeled in addition. The college student case study (Section 4.7.2) shows a worked example.




Hurlbert, S.H. (1984) “Pseudoreplication and the design of ecological field experiments,” Ecological Monographs, 54(2), pp. 187–211. Available at: https://doi.org/10.2307/1942661.


4.2.2 The random slope model
A second effect that we could imagine is that the effect of standLRT is different for each school. As a fixed effect model, we would express this, for example, as lm(normexam ~ standLRT*school + sex)
The random effect equivalent is called the random slope model. A random slope model assumes that each school also gets their own slope for a given parameter (per default we will always estimate slope and intercept, but you could overwrite this, not recommended!). Let’s do this for standLRT (you could of course fit random slopes on both predictors as well).

mod2 = lmer(normexam ~ standLRT + sex +  (standLRT | school), data = Exam)
summary(mod2)

Linear mixed model fit by REML ['lmerMod']
Formula: normexam ~ standLRT + sex + (standLRT | school)
   Data: Exam

REML criterion at convergence: 9303.2

Scaled residuals: 
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-3.8339 -0.6373  0.0245  0.6819  3.4500 

Random effects:
 Groups   Name        Variance Std.Dev. Corr 
 school   (Intercept) 0.08795  0.2966        
          standLRT    0.01514  0.1230   0.53 
 Residual             0.55019  0.7417        
Number of obs: 4059, groups:  school, 65

Fixed effects:
            Estimate Std. Error t value
(Intercept)  0.06389    0.04167   1.533
standLRT     0.55275    0.02016  27.420
sexM        -0.17576    0.03228  -5.445

Correlation of Fixed Effects:
         (Intr) stnLRT
standLRT  0.356       
sexM     -0.334  0.036


Again, the difference to the fixed effect model is that in the random effect model, we assume that the variance between slopes comes from a normal distribution. The result is similar to the random intercept model, except that we have an additional variance term for the slopes, and a correlation between random intercepts and random slopes (Corr in the output).






TipGenerate equation with the equatiomatic package





We can use the equatiomatic package to print LaTeX code for the underlying equation of our random slope model:

library(equatiomatic)
extract_eq(mod2)

\[\begin{aligned}
  \operatorname{normexam}_{i}  &\sim N \left(\alpha_{j[i]} + \beta_{1j[i]}(\operatorname{standLRT}) + \beta_{2}(\operatorname{sex}_{\operatorname{M}}), \sigma^2 \right) \\    
\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    \begin{aligned}
      &\alpha_{j} \\
      &\beta_{1j}
    \end{aligned}
  \end{array}
\right)
  &\sim N \left(
\left(
  \begin{array}{c}
    \begin{aligned}
      &\mu_{\alpha_{j}} \\
      &\mu_{\beta_{1j}}
    \end{aligned}
  \end{array}
\right)
,
\left(
  \begin{array}{cc}
     \sigma^2_{\alpha_{j}} & \rho_{\alpha_{j}\beta_{1j}} \\
     \rho_{\beta_{1j}\alpha_{j}} & \sigma^2_{\beta_{1j}}
  \end{array}
\right)
\right)
    \text{, for school j = 1,} \dots \text{,J}
\end{aligned}\]



Here a visualization of the results

with(Exam, {
  randcoefI = ranef(mod2)$school[,1]
  randcoefS = ranef(mod2)$school[,2]
  fixedcoef = fixef(mod2)
  plot(standLRT, normexam)
    for(i in 1:65){
      abline(a = fixedcoef[1] + randcoefI[i] , b = fixedcoef[2] + randcoefS[i], col = i)
    }
})










4.2.3 Mixed models in different packages

4.2.3.1 lme4 / glmmTMB
There are a large number of packages to fit mixed models in R. The main packages that you use, because they are most user-friendly and stable, are lme4 and glmmTMB. They share more or less the same syntax for random effects.

Random intercept: (1 | group).
ONLY random slope for a given fixed effect: (0 + fixedEffect | group).
Random slope + intercept + correlation (default): (fixedEffect | group).
Random slope + intercept without correlation: (fixedEffect || group), identical to
(1 | group) + (0 + fixedEffect | group) (for a numeric fixedEffect; for a factor, lme4 still estimates the correlations between its levels).
Nested random effects: (1 | group / subgroup). If groups are labeled A, B, C, … and subgroups 1, 2, 3, …, this will create labels A1, A2 ,B1, B2, so that you effectively group in subgroups. Useful for the many experimental people that do not label subgroups uniquely, but otherwise no statistical difference to a normal (crossed) random effect.
Crossed random effects: You can add random effects independently, as in
(1 | group1) + (1 | group2).







Tip 4.2: More on crossed vs. nested REs





There is often confusion about the behavior and meaning of crossed vs. nested REs. From the statistical / mathematical side, there is no difference between them, there are just REs. Crossed vs. nested is a shorthand to tell you how the data was coded.
Let’s look at the Exam data, for example. If you run

table(Exam$student, Exam$school)

you will see that the student ID = 1 appears in many schools. Clearly, this cannot be the same student, the reason is that each school uses their own ID. If you would fit a crossed RE, as in

m1 = lmer(normexam ~ standLRT + sex +  (1 | school) + (1 |student), data = Exam)
summary(m1)

you would fit a common effect for each student with ID = 1. This, however, doesn’t make sense, there is no connection between these students. Thus, you should fit

m2 = lmer(normexam ~ standLRT + sex +  (1 | school/student), data = Exam)
summary(m2)

Compare the number of RE groups in the summary: in m1, you have 650 students. In m2, you have 4055 student:school levels for the RE. Thus, the nested syntax makes sure that students with the same ID in different schools are treated as different individuals.
You could fit the same mod by changing the coding of student. To do this, we create a new variable, combining school and student into a unique ID

Exam$uniqueStudent = as.factor(paste(Exam$school, "-", Exam$student))

m3 = lmer(normexam ~ standLRT + sex +  (1 | school) + (1|uniqueStudent), data = Exam)
summary(m3)

If you check the summary of m3, now we also have 4055 levels for uniqueStudent, and the results are identical to the nested model version.
Caution: in the Exam data, almost every student appears only once (4055 student:school levels for 4059 observations), so a student-level RE cannot be separated from the residual error; the fit is singular (sd of student:school = 0). The example only illustrates the coding. Nested REs make sense if the lower level is replicated.





4.2.3.2 nlme
nlme is a classic package for fitting (nonlinear) mixed effect models. I would argue that it is largely superseded by lme4 and glmmTMB, but it still offers a few special tricks that are not available in either lme4 or glmmTMB. A linear mixed model with random intercept in nlme looks like this

nlme::lme(Resp ~ Predictor, random = ~1|Group, data = data)



4.2.3.3 mgcv
If you want to use GAMs, there is basically only mgcv (or brms, if you’re willing to go Bayesian).

# Group must be a factor
mgcv::gam(Resp ~ Predictor + s(Group, bs = 're'), data = data)



4.2.3.4 brms
brms is a very interesting package that allows you to estimate mixed models via Bayesian Inference with STAN.

brm_mod <- brms::brm(Resp ~ Predictor + (1|Group),
                     data = data) # add e.g. family = poisson for GLMMs, see the chapter on GLMs
summary(brm_mod)

A complete brms GLMM is shown in the owls exercise (Caution 9.2). For an introduction to Bayesian mixed models, see the chapter on linear and linear mixed models in Hartig (2024).

Hartig, F. (2024) “Introduction to Bayesian statistics with R.” Available at: https://florianhartig.github.io/LearningBayes/.



4.2.4 REML vs. MLE
Frequentist linear mixed models are usually estimated with REML = restricted maximum likelihood, rather than with classical MLE. Most packages allow you to switch between REML and MLE. The motivation for REML is that for limited data (non-asymptotics), the MLE for variance components of the model are typically negatively biased, because the uncertainty of the fixed effects is not properly accounted for. If you go through the mathematics, you can make an analogy to the bias-corrected sampling variance (Bates, 2011).

Bates, D. (2011) “Computational methods for mixed models,” Vignette for lme4 [Preprint].
REML maximizes the likelihood of linear combinations of the data that do not depend on the fixed effects (equivalently, the likelihood after integrating out the fixed effects). This accounts for the df used by the fixed effects, like dividing by n-p instead of n when estimating a variance in a linear model.
Most packages offer an option to switch between REML and ML estimation of the model. In lme4, this is done via

m = lmer(normexam ~ standLRT + sex +  (1 | school), data = Exam)
m = lmer(normexam ~ standLRT + sex +  (1 | school), data = Exam, REML = F)

Regarding when to use what, use the following rule of thumb:

Per default, use REML
Switch to ML (REML = FALSE) if you compare models with different fixed effects, or a mixed model with a model without random effects, via LRTs or AIC. For comparing RE structures with identical fixed effects, REML is fine.







Tip



Later in this chapter (Section 4.5.3), we will talk about model selection via LRTs and AIC. Because those depend on the likelihood, it is generally recommended to switch from REML to ML in this case. The reason is that the REML likelihood refers to linear combinations of the data that do not depend on the fixed effects, i.e. to different data when the fixed-effect structure changes, so REML likelihoods are not comparable between models with different fixed effects. I would recommend sticking to this, although I have to say that I have always wondered how big this problem is, compared to the other df problems associated to mixed models (see Section 4.5.1).








Caution 4.1: Exercise — A mixed model for plantHeight



Take the plantHeight model that we worked with already in the exercise in the chapter on linear regression (Caution 2.1):

library(EcoData)

oldModel <- lm(loght ~ temp, data = plantHeight)
summary(oldModel)

We have one observation per species. Consider that the relationship height ~ temp may be different for each family. Some families may have larger plants in general (random intercept), but it may also be that the temperature relationship changes per family (random slope). Run these two models for our problem.








TipSolution






# Random intercept model

library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)
randomInterceptModel <- lmer(loght ~ temp + (1|Family), data = plantHeight)
summary(randomInterceptModel)

# Random slope model

randomSlopeModel <- lmer(loght ~ temp + (temp | Family), data = plantHeight)
summary(randomSlopeModel)

# scaling helps the optimizer
plantHeight$sTemp = scale(plantHeight$temp)

randomSlopeModel <- lmer(loght ~ sTemp + (sTemp | Family), data = plantHeight)
summary(randomSlopeModel)

title: 4  Linear mixed models
section: 4.3 Advantages and interpretation of random effects
text:
4.3 Advantages and interpretation of random effects



What do the random effects mean, and why should we use them?

4.3.1 Interpretation
The classical interpretation of the random intercept is that they model a group-structured residual error, i.e. they are like residuals, but for an entire group. However, this view breaks down a bit for a random slope model.
Another view this is that REs terms absorb group-structured variation in model parameters. This view works for random intercept and slope models. So, our main model fits the grand mean, and the RE models variation in the parameters, which is assumed to be normally distributed.
A third view of RE models is that they are regularized fixed effect models. What does that mean? Note again that, conceptually, every random effect model corresponds to a fixed effect model. For a random intercept model, this would be

lmer(y ~ x + (1|group)) => lm(y ~ x + group)

and for the random slope, it would be

lmer(y ~ x + (x|group)) => lm(y ~ x * group)

So, alternatively to a mixed model, we could always fit a fixed effect model, and that would also take care of the variation in groups. Of course, the output of the two models differs, but that’s just what people programmed. The real difference, however, is that by making the assumption that the random effects come from a normal distribution, we are imposing a constraint on the estimates, which creates a shrinkage on the fitted REs (see Section 4.3.2).


4.3.2 RE shrinkage
To understand shrinkage, note that whatever the fitted sd of the normal distribution underlying the RE, as long as it is finite, it will always be more likely that the RE estimate is at zero (i.e. the grand mean) than at 1 or 2 sd. This means that RE estimates are biased towards the grand mean.
We can visualize the effect by comparing estimates of a fixed to a random effect model

mf = lm(normexam ~ 0 + school, data = Exam)
mr = lmer(normexam ~ (1 | school), data = Exam)

ef = coef(mf)
er = ranef(mr)$school$`(Intercept)`
plot(ef, er, xlab = "fixed", ylab = "random")
abline(0,1)








The plot shows that random effect estimates are biased towards the grand mean, i.e. positive values are lower than in the LM, and negative values are higher than in the LM. This is called shrinkage.






Note



The shrinkage imposed by the RE is equivalent to an L2 (ridge) regression (see Section 8.2.3), or a normally distributed Bayesian prior. You can see this by considering that the log likelihood of a normal distribution is equivalent to a quadratic penalty for deviations from the mean. The difference is that the strength of the penalty, controlled by the RE sd, is estimated. For that reason, the RE shrinkage is also referred to as an example of “adaptive shrinkage”.


This RE shrinkage is useful in many situations, beyond describing a group-structured error in the data. A common use is that by using a random slope model, parameter estimates for groups with few data points are drawn towards the grand mean and thus informed by the estimates of the other groups. For example, if we have data for common and rare species, and we are interested in the density dependence of the species, we could fit a random slope for density per species. Consider the plantHeight case study we did in the exercise in the chapter on linear regression (Caution 2.2). We saw that, even after re-leveling the predictor, not all interactions could be estimated, because some factor levels had only one observation.

library(EcoData)
plantHeight$growthform2 = relevel(as.factor(plantHeight$growthform), "Herb")
plantHeight$sTemp = scale(plantHeight$temp)
fit <- lm(loght ~ sTemp * growthform2 , data = plantHeight)
summary(fit)

If you run the same thing as a random slope model, you will see that we can estimate a random intercept and slope for each growth form, even those that have only one observation

fit <- lmer(loght ~ sTemp + (sTemp | growthform2) , data = plantHeight)
ranef(fit)

$growthform2
           (Intercept)       sTemp
Herb       -0.70060787  0.07032554
Fern       -0.07771756  0.01484118
Herb/Shrub -0.18519919  0.03351554
Shrub      -0.17681675  0.11176808
Shrub/Tree  0.29044226 -0.04361958
Tree        0.84989911 -0.18683076

with conditional variances for "growthform2" 


The reason is that rare growth forms will be constrained by the RE, while common growth forms with a lot of data can overrule the normal distribution imposed by the random slope and get their own estimate. In this picture, the random effect imposes an adaptive shrinkage, similar to a ridge shrinkage estimator, with the shrinkage strength controlled by the standard deviation of the random effect. An alternative view is that the RE variance acts as a prior distribution on the slope. Of course, the estimates are biased towards the grand mean, so if you want to interpret these estimates that is a cost that you have to take into account.


4.3.3 When to use what?
So, to finalize this discussion: there are essentially two main differences between a random vs. fixed effect model

In the RE model, we are fitting a grand mean and differences from the grand mean, while in the fixed effect model, we have to set up contrasts (various options, see Section 2.6.1), with treatment contrasts as defaults
The LM (OLS) is mathematically proven to be the best linear unbiased estimator (BLUE) of the regression problem. In a mixed model, REs (but not fixed effects) are biased towards the grand mean, but the advantage is that the random effect loses fewer degrees of freedom, i.e. the power on the fixed effects will be higher.

While point 1 is more a choice about how to report results (in principle, we could also calculate the grand mean for fixed effect group estimates), the second point (higher power) is a clear advantage in many cases, in particular if you don’t care about the bias on the REs. Therefore, the rule of thumb for REs is:

If you have a categorical variable, and you’re not interested in its estimates, model it as a RE
If you want to get unbiased estimates of the categorical variable (or its interactions), use a fixed effect

A common question is how many levels a grouping variable needs to be modeled as a random effect. Because the variance of a random effect is estimated from its levels, a common rule of thumb is to use at least about 5-10 levels, and to model a grouping variable with fewer levels as a fixed effect (Bolker, 2015; Harrison et al., 2018). With few levels, the variance estimate is indeed imprecise and biased towards zero, and singular fits are common. However, if you are interested in the population-level effect of a predictor rather than in the individual levels, simulations by Oberpriller, Souza Leite and Pichler (2022) suggest that a mixed model can still give reliable tests, provided that singular fits are handled. They recommend to start with a mixed model regardless of the number of levels. If the effect of the predictor varies between groups, start with a correlated random slope and intercept; after a singular fit, remove the correlation (||, see Section 4.4.1), and if the fit is still singular, switch to a fixed effect. In their simulations, singular mixed models had inflated type I error rates, similar to a model that omits the grouping variable, and omitting random slopes that are present in the data also inflated the type I error. In short, with few levels both options can be defended, and more levels are clearly better, so when planning a study, aim for more than the minimum.

Bolker, B.M. (2015) “Linear and generalized linear mixed models,” in Ecological statistics. Oxford University Press, pp. 309–333. Available at: https://doi.org/10.1093/acprof:oso/9780199672547.003.0014.

Harrison, X.A. et al. (2018) “A brief introduction to mixed effects modelling and multi-model inference in ecology,” PeerJ, 6, p. e4794. Available at: https://doi.org/10.7717/peerj.4794.
The choice between a random and a fixed effect based on whether you are interested in the estimates is just a rule of thumb; in data-poor situations, it is common to use random slope models and interpret the estimates as well. In this case, we are using the RE to optimize the bias-variance trade-off (see the section on the bias-variance trade-off in the model selection chapter, Section 8.1).

title: 4  Linear mixed models
text:
4.4 Model checks



As residual checks for an LMM, you should first of all check for everything that you would check in an LM, i.e. you would expect that the residual distribution is iid normal. On top of that, you should check the REs for:

Convergence (mixed models often have convergence problems)
Normality
Correlation with predictors -> RE can mask misfit
Residual patterns -> evidence for random slope

I will show all of those using the example

mod1 = lmer(normexam ~ standLRT + sex +  (1 | school), data = Exam)
summary(mod1)

Linear mixed model fit by REML ['lmerMod']
Formula: normexam ~ standLRT + sex + (1 | school)
   Data: Exam

REML criterion at convergence: 9346.6

Scaled residuals: 
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-3.7120 -0.6314  0.0166  0.6855  3.2735 

Random effects:
 Groups   Name        Variance Std.Dev.
 school   (Intercept) 0.08986  0.2998  
 Residual             0.56252  0.7500  
Number of obs: 4059, groups:  school, 65

Fixed effects:
            Estimate Std. Error t value
(Intercept)  0.07639    0.04202   1.818
standLRT     0.55947    0.01245  44.930
sexM        -0.17136    0.03279  -5.226

Correlation of Fixed Effects:
         (Intr) stnLRT
standLRT -0.013       
sexM     -0.337  0.061



4.4.1 Convergence
If there is a convergence problem, you should usually get a warning. Other signs of convergence problems may be RE estimates that are zero, CIs that are extremely large, or strong correlations in the correlation matrix of the predictors that is reported by summary(). Here, we have no problems, but we’ll see examples of this as we go on.
There are different types of convergence problems that you can encounter:

Warnings about scaling and centering -> just do it, it doesn’t cost you!
The warning “boundary (singular) fit: see help(‘isSingular’)” (meaning that some dimensions of the variance-covariance matrix have been estimated to zero. -> often, this just means that a RE estimate is zero. In many cases, this is not a problem and can actually be ignored, but it is hard to give general advice to when this is the case. With few levels in the grouping variable, however, a singular fit can inflate the type I error of the fixed effects (Oberpriller, Souza Leite and Pichler, 2022); see the recommendations in Section 4.3.3. In random slope models, it often helps to move from | to || (suppressing the correlation). Removing the RE will solve the problem, but could lead to type I error inflation. A more conservative solution would be to change the RE to a fixed effect
Optimizer / convergence warnings: use lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa", optCtrl = list(maxfun = 1e5)) (glmerControl() for glmer) to change the optimizer to bobyqa and possibly increase the number of iterations, e.g. lmer(..., control = lmerControl(optimizer = "bobyqa", optCtrl = list(maxfun = 1e5))).


Oberpriller, J., Souza Leite, M. de and Pichler, M. (2022) “Fixed or random? On the reliability of mixed-effects models for a small number of levels in grouping variables,” Ecology and Evolution, 12(7), p. e9062. Available at: https://doi.org/10.1002/ece3.9062.


4.4.2 Observation-level residual plots
Unfortunately, lme4 plots only provide res ~ fitted as default

plot(mod1)








For a qqplot, you have to calculate the residuals by hand

qqnorm(residuals(mod1))
qqline(residuals(mod1))








Of course, any time you do a qqnorm plot, you could also run a shapiro.test to get a p-value for the deviation from normality (interpret visually: such tests are over-sensitive for large n and underpowered for few groups). You can also use the DHARMa plots

library(DHARMa)
res <- simulateResiduals(mod1, plot = T)








Both plots look fine. Of course, we should also check residuals against predictors. In DHARMa, we can do this via

par(mfrow = c(1,2))
plotResiduals(res, Exam$standLRT)
plotResiduals(res, Exam$sex)














Tip 4.3: Conditional, unconditional and marginal predictions



For mixed models, there are three ways to make predictions, which are easy to confuse:

Conditional predictions include the estimated random effects, i.e. they are the predictions for the particular groups in the data (re.form = NULL in lme4, the default).
Unconditional predictions use only the fixed effects, i.e. the random effects are set to zero (re.form = NA or re.form = ~0). This is the prediction for an “average” group.
Marginal predictions are averaged over the distribution of the random effects, i.e. the mean prediction over all possible groups.

In a linear mixed model, unconditional and marginal predictions are identical, because the random effects average to zero. With a nonlinear link function (GLMMs), they differ (see Section 9.5.1). Note that these terms are not used consistently in the literature and in R packages; e.g. the “marginal R2” of mixed models (Section 4.5.4) is based on the fixed effects only.








Tip 4.4: Conditional vs. unconditional predictions and residuals



When you predict with a random effect model, you can do conditional or unconditional predictions (see Tip 4.3). The difference is that conditional predictions include the REs, while unconditional predictions only include the fixed effects.

predict(mod1, re.form = NULL) # conditional, default
predict(mod1, re.form = ~0) # unconditional

This also makes a difference for the residual calculations: in principle, you could calculate residuals with respect to both predictions. In lme4, however, residuals() always returns conditional residuals (observed minus conditional predictions). It has no re.form argument, and additional arguments are silently ignored, so residuals(mod1, re.form = ~0) would still give conditional residuals. Unconditional residuals have to be calculated by hand with predict():

residuals(mod1) # conditional
Exam$normexam - predict(mod1, re.form = NULL) # conditional, same as residuals(mod1)
Exam$normexam - predict(mod1, re.form = ~0) # unconditional

DHARMa offers both: since version 0.5.0, simulateResiduals() simulates conditional on the fitted random effects by default, and with simulateREs = "unconditional" it re-simulates them. Both have advantages and disadvantages:

Conditional residuals are more sensitive to violations of the iid normal assumptions of the outer (observation-level) normal error
However, REs can sometimes absorb misfit, such that plotting conditional residuals ~ pred looks fine, but unconditional ~ pred does not. For that reason, if you only check conditional residuals, you should also check REs ~ pred (see Section 4.4.4)





4.4.3 Normality of REs
I prefer to look at this visually. You can also run a shapiro.test() to check if you should consider the pattern at all, but interpret it visually: such tests are over-sensitive for large n and underpowered for few groups.

x = ranef(mod1)
qqnorm(x$school$`(Intercept)`)








Question is how bad can this be? (Neuhaus, McCulloch and Boylan, 2013) report some simulation results that suggest that fixed effect slopes (bias, coverage) are relatively robust to misspecification in the RE distribution, which is reassuring.

Neuhaus, J.M., McCulloch, C.E. and Boylan, R. (2013) “Estimation of covariate effects in generalized linear mixed models with a misspecified distribution of random intercepts and slopes,” Statistics in Medicine, 32(14), pp. 2419–2429. Available at: https://doi.org/10.1002/sim.5682.


4.4.4 Correlation of REs with predictors
As mentioned in Tip 4.4, REs can sometimes absorb misfit of the fixed effect structure. It can therefore be useful to check if there is a correlation with the predictors, especially if you only check conditional residuals. Example:

y = aggregate(standLRT ~ school, FUN = mean, data = Exam)
plot(x$school$`(Intercept)` ~ y$standLRT)








A trend of the school intercepts with the school mean of a predictor means that the RE absorbs an effect that should be in the fixed part. Here, there is a weak positive trend (correlation about 0.35): schools with a higher average reading score tend to have higher intercepts. A common remedy is to add the school mean of the predictor as an additional fixed effect (in Exam it already exists as schavg), which separates the within-school from the between-school effect.


4.4.5 Residual pattern per group
lme4 has an excellent plot syntax to plot residuals per grouping factor. Check out the help of plot.merMod. The following plot shows residuals ~ fitted for each school

plot(mod1, resid(., scaled=TRUE) ~ standLRT | school, abline = 0)








Looks still good to me, but if we think we see a pattern here, we should introduce a random slope.

title: 4  Linear mixed models
text:
4.5 Downstream analysis of mixed models



Specifying mixed models is quite simple, but their practical application raises several issues (degrees of freedom, model selection, ANOVA, predictions). The following table gives an overview of how to obtain tests and confidence intervals for mixed models; the subsections of this section explain the details. The columns for glmer and glmmTMB become relevant for generalized linear mixed models (Section 9.5).



Table 4.1: Tests and confidence intervals for mixed models.












Question
lmer
glmer
glmmTMB
Section

t-test with approximate df (summary() after loading lmerTest)
Wald z-test (summary())
Wald z-test (summary())
Section 4.5.1

F-test with approximate df (anova() after loading lmerTest, type III); alternatives in Section 4.5.4

car::Anova() (Wald \(\chi^2\))
Section 4.5.4

emmeans() with pairs() or contrast()
emmeans()
emmeans()

anova(m0, m1)

Section 4.5.3.1

simulated LRT
Section 4.5.3.3


CIs for fixed effects
confint() (profile); for few groups (fewer than about 10-20), parametric bootstrap (confint() of a bootMer() result)
confint() (profile; method = "Wald" is faster)
confint() (Wald; method = "profile" is also available)
Section 4.5.1


CIs for random effect standard deviations
confint() (profile)
confint() (profile)
confint() (Wald, listed as Std.Dev.)
Section 4.5.1


CIs for predictions
parametric bootstrap with bootMer() (the prediction function also needs re.form = NA); approximate: predict(..., se.fit = TRUE) (lme4 2.0 or later)
as for lmer
predict(..., se.fit = TRUE, re.form = NA); compute the CI on the link scale and back-transform
Section 4.5.2






All of these are approximations, because the degrees of freedom of a mixed model are not clearly defined (Section 4.5.1). With few groups (as a rule of thumb, fewer than about 10-20), Wald tests and also likelihood ratio tests with the standard \(\chi^2\) distribution give p-values for fixed effects that are too small. For linear mixed models, the approximate degrees of freedom of lmerTest (Satterthwaite) or Kenward-Roger (car::Anova(m, test.statistic = "F")) are then more reliable; for GLMMs, use a parametric bootstrap or a simulated LRT (DHARMa::simulateLRT(), pbkrtest::PBmodcomp()), and profile instead of Wald CIs. In contrast, a standard likelihood ratio test for a random effect is conservative, because the null hypothesis (variance = 0) lies at the boundary of the parameter space, which is another reason to use the simulated LRT. Finally, note that anova() after loading lmerTest gives type III tests, while car::Anova() gives type II tests by default; with interactions, they test different hypotheses (Section 3.2.3, Caution 4.2), so say which one you report.

4.5.1 Degrees of freedom for a random effect
Possibly the most central problem is: How many parameters does a random effect model have?






Note



Why is it so important to know how many parameters a model has? The answer is that what seems like a very minor point is needed in all the mathematics for calculating p-values, AIC, LRTs and all that, so without knowing the complexity of the model, the mathematics that is used in lm() breaks down.


We can make some guesses about the complexity of an LMM by looking at its fixed effect version counterparts:

mFix0 = lm(normexam ~ standLRT + sex , data = Exam)
mFix0$rank # 3 parameters.

mRE = lmer(normexam ~ standLRT + sex +  (1 | school), data = Exam)
# No idea how many parameters.

mFixSchool = lm(normexam ~ standLRT + sex + school, data = Exam)
mFixSchool$rank # 67 parameters.

So, we see that the fixed effect model without school has 3 parameters, and with school 67. It is reasonable to assume that the complexity of the mixed model is somewhere in-between, because it fits the same effects as mFixSchool, but they are constrained by the normal distribution.
The width of this normal distribution is controlled by the estimated variance of the random effect. For a high variance, the normal is very wide, and the mixed model is nearly as complex as mFixSchool; but for a low variance, the normal is very narrow, and the mixed model it is only as complex as mFix0. The shrinkage plot in Section 4.3.2 shows this directly: the more the random estimates are pulled towards the grand mean, the fewer effective parameters the model uses.






Note



Technically, the mixed model mRE estimates the same 65 school effects as the fixed effect model mFixSchool, plus one more parameter, the standard deviation of the random effects. Could it thus ever be more flexible than mFixSchool? The answer is no - the RE standard deviation is what is technically called a hyperparameter. It is not an effect that is estimated, but rather a parameter that controls the freedom of the estimated effects, so the effective number of parameters of the mixed model can never exceed that of mFixSchool.


Because of these issues, lmer by default does not return p-values (for an overview of the options, see Table 4.1). The help advises you to use bootstrapping to generate valid confidence intervals and p-values on parameters. This is possible indeed, but very cumbersome.
However, you can calculate p-values based on approximate degrees of freedom via the lmerTest package, which also corrects ANOVA for random effects, but not AIC.

library(lmerTest)

m2 = lmer(normexam ~ standLRT + sex +  (1 | school), data = Exam)
summary(m2)

Linear mixed model fit by REML. t-tests use Satterthwaite's method [
lmerModLmerTest]

Number of obs: 4059, groups:  school, 65

confint(m2)

.sig01       0.245031246  0.3645283
