(Intercept)   0.1619     0.2740   0.591    0.555


If you check the results, you can see that

Both models correctly estimate the AR1 parameter
The p-value for the intercept is in both models n.s., as expected







NoteResidual checks conditional on the fitted random effects



glmmTMB fits the AR1 structure as a random effect, with one value per time point. When DHARMa simulates new data to calculate residuals, the question is whether these random effects are re-simulated (unconditional simulations) or kept at their fitted values (conditional simulations, see also Tip 4.3). Since DHARMa 0.5.0, simulateResiduals() simulates conditionally by default. For glmmTMB models, DHARMa does this via glmmTMB::set_simcodes(fit$obj, val = "fix"); for a few covariance structures, this is not yet possible, and DHARMa then falls back to unconditional simulations with a message. With simulateREs = "unconditional", all random effects are re-simulated. To simulate conditionally directly with glmmTMB:

glmmTMB::set_simcodes(fitGLMMTMB$obj, val = "fix") # note: this modifies the model object
simulate(fitGLMMTMB, nsim = 10)

Let’s compare the two options for our AR1 model:

resU = simulateResiduals(fitGLMMTMB, simulateREs = "unconditional")
testTemporalAutocorrelation(resU, time = 1:1000)









    Durbin-Watson test

data:  simulationOutput$scaledResiduals ~ 1
DW = 0.24923, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true autocorrelation is not 0

resC = simulateResiduals(fitGLMMTMB) # conditional (default)
testTemporalAutocorrelation(resC, time = 1:1000)









    Durbin-Watson test

data:  simulationOutput$scaledResiduals ~ 1
DW = 2.8049, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true autocorrelation is not 0


The unconditional residuals still contain the full autocorrelation, because the AR1 process is re-simulated, so they cannot tell us whether the AR1 model is adequate. The conditional residuals no longer show the positive autocorrelation, but a negative one (Durbin-Watson statistic > 2): with one random effect per time point, the fitted random effects also absorb part of the independent noise, so the conditional residuals are not independent either. Therefore, use DHARMa’s autocorrelation test mainly on the model without a correlation structure, to decide whether you need one. To check the fitted AR1 model, a cleaner option for normal responses are the normalized residuals of gls, from which the estimated correlation has been removed:

acf(residuals(fitGLS, type = "normalized"))
















NoteWhy de-trending is important





As discussed in Section 11.1.1, a misfit trend also creates residual autocorrelation. Let’s simulate data with a nonlinear time trend, but with independent residuals, i.e. without any autocorrelation:

set.seed(123)
time = 1:1000/100
y = time + 2*sin(time/0.4) + rnorm(1000)
data = data.frame(y = y, time = time)
plot(y ~ time, data = data)








If we only remove a linear trend, the residuals are strongly autocorrelated, because the sine wave that we did not model is still in them:

fit1 = lm(y ~ time, data = data)
res1 = simulateResiduals(fit1, plot = TRUE)







testTemporalAutocorrelation(res1, time = data$time)









    Durbin-Watson test

data:  simulationOutput$scaledResiduals ~ 1
DW = 0.62908, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: true autocorrelation is not 0


The correct reaction is not to add an AR1 structure, but to de-trend properly, e.g. with a spline (Section 2.5.3):

library(mgcv)
fit2 = gam(y ~ s(time), data = data)
res2 = simulateResiduals(fit2, plot = TRUE)







testTemporalAutocorrelation(res2, time = data$time)









    Durbin-Watson test

data:  simulationOutput$scaledResiduals ~ 1
DW = 1.9629, p-value = 0.5574
alternative hypothesis: true autocorrelation is not 0


After de-trending, the residuals look fine and there is no autocorrelation left, so we don’t need a correlation structure.
What would have happened if we had added an AR1 structure to the linear model instead?

fit3 = gls(y ~ time, correlation = corAR1(form = ~ 1), data = data, method = "ML")
summary(fit3)

The AR1 model estimates a considerable autocorrelation (Phi), although there is none in the data: the correlation structure absorbs the misfit of the trend. In this case, the AR1 model is inappropriate. It interprets a systematic trend as random correlated noise, it fits much worse than the GAM (AIC), and its normalized residuals are still not independent (check acf(residuals(fit3, type = "normalized"))). An AR1 structure is meant for the autocorrelation that remains after the trend has been removed, not as a replacement for de-trending.




11.2.1 Exercise — Hurricanes revisited?






CautionExercise



Look at the hurricane study that we also analyze in the case studies (Section C.1), which is, after all, temporal data. This data set is located in DHARMa.

library(DHARMa)

fit = glmmTMB(alldeaths ~ scale(MasFem) *
                          (scale(Minpressure_Updated_2014) + scale(NDAM)),
                           data = hurricanes, family = nbinom2)

# Residual checks with DHARMa.
res = simulateResiduals(fit)

# Checking for temporal autocorrelation
res2 = recalculateResiduals(res, group = hurricanes$Year)
testTemporalAutocorrelation(res2, time = unique(hurricanes$Year))









    Durbin-Watson test

data:  simulationOutput$scaledResiduals ~ 1
DW = 2.5518, p-value = 0.04758
alternative hypothesis: true autocorrelation is not 0


We see that there is a tiny bit of autocorrelation. Note that this autocorrelation is negative, so if we have a higher residual in one year, it is lower in the next year. Normally, we would expect temporal autocorrelation to be positive, so this is a bit weird. It could be an effect of people being more careful if there were many fatalities in the previous year, but it could also be a statistical fluke.
In any case, as an exercise, we want to address the issue - add an AR1 term to the model!








TipSolution





Adding the AR1 to the glmmTMB model

hurricanes$yearF <- factor(hurricanes$Year)
hurricanes$group = factor(rep(1,nrow(hurricanes)))

fit = glmmTMB(alldeaths ~ scale(MasFem) *
                          (scale(Minpressure_Updated_2014) + scale(NDAM))
                          + ar1(yearF + 0 | group),
                           data = hurricanes, family = nbinom2)

Note that ar1 on a factor treats consecutive years in the data as lag 1, although there are gaps between the years (49 distinct years between 1950 and 2012); for irregular times, glmmTMB offers the continuous-time analogue ou(numFactor(Year) + 0 | group).
Careful, we are getting a convergence warning here! You should take these warnings seriously! The estimated variance of the AR1 term is practically zero (a boundary estimate), so the reported correlation (positive, although the residual test indicated negative autocorrelation) is meaningless. Let’s fit a reduced model:

The reduced model converges and estimates a weak negative autocorrelation (about -0.24), but of course this is not the model we want. Changing the optimizer (see Section 4.4.1) does not help for the full model: the variance of the AR1 term stays at the boundary. With only a borderline residual test (and we ran many tests) and a negligible AIC gain in the reduced model (707.6 with vs 708.6 without the AR1 term), there is no convincing evidence for temporal autocorrelation, so we would stay with the model without AR1 term. A correlation structure that the data do not support typically shows up as convergence problems.

title: 11  Correlation structures
text:
11.3 Spatial correlation structures



Spatial models work very similarly to the temporal models. This time, we start directly with an example, using a data set with the thickness of coal seams, that we try to predict with a spatial (soil) predictor.

library(EcoData)
plot(thick ~ soil, data = thickness)








Let’s fit a simple LM to this

fit = lm(thick ~ soil, data = thickness)
summary(fit)


Call:
lm(formula = thick ~ soil, data = thickness)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-6.0414 -1.1975  0.0876  1.4836  4.9584 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept)  31.9420     3.1570  10.118 1.54e-15 ***
soil          2.2552     0.8656   2.605   0.0111 *  
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 2.278 on 73 degrees of freedom
Multiple R-squared:  0.08508,   Adjusted R-squared:  0.07254 
F-statistic: 6.788 on 1 and 73 DF,  p-value: 0.01111


DHARMa checks:

res = simulateResiduals(fit)
testSpatialAutocorrelation(res, x = thickness$north, y = thickness$east)









    DHARMa Moran's I test for distance-based autocorrelation

data:  res
observed = 0.210870, expected = -0.013514, sd = 0.021940, p-value <
2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: Distance-based autocorrelation


For spatial data, we often look at spatial variograms, which are similar to an acf but in spatial directions

library(gstat)
tann.dir.vgm = variogram(residuals(fit) ~ 1,
                         loc =~ east + north, data = thickness,
                         alpha = c(0, 45, 90, 135))
plot(tann.dir.vgm)








How to read a variogram: the x-axis is the distance between pairs of points, the y-axis the semivariance (half the mean squared difference between the residuals of pairs at that distance); for independent residuals the curve is flat, autocorrelation shows as a low semivariance at short distances that increases with distance and then levels off. A curve that keeps rising without leveling off, or that differs between the four directions, indicates a large-scale trend. Both the DHARMa plots and the variograms are more indicative of a spatial trend. Let’s remove this with a 2d-spline, called a tensor spline:

library(mgcv)

fit1 = gam(thick ~ soil + te(east, north) , data = thickness)
summary(fit1)


Family: gaussian 
Link function: identity 

Formula:
thick ~ soil + te(east, north)

Parametric coefficients:

---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

R-sq.(adj) =  0.996   Deviance explained = 99.7%
GCV = 0.033201  Scale est. = 0.022981  n = 75

plot(fit1, pages = 0, lwd = 2)








We can check the model again, and the problem is gone (the test is no longer significant)

res = simulateResiduals(fit1)
testSpatialAutocorrelation(res, x = thickness$north, y = thickness$east)









    DHARMa Moran's I test for distance-based autocorrelation

data:  res
observed = -0.024242, expected = -0.013514, sd = 0.021860, p-value =
0.6236
alternative hypothesis: Distance-based autocorrelation


If we had still seen a signal, we should have fit an autoregressive model. Here it’s not necessary, but just to show you the syntax - first nlme:

fit2 = gls(thick ~ soil , correlation = corExp(form =~ east + north) , data = thickness)
summary(fit2)

Generalized least squares fit by REML
  Model: thick ~ soil 
  Data: thickness 
       AIC      BIC    logLik
  164.3474 173.5092 -78.17368

Correlation Structure: Exponential spatial correlation
 Formula: ~east + north 
 Parameter estimate(s):
   range 
719.4121 

Coefficients:
               Value Std.Error  t-value p-value
(Intercept) 42.81488  5.314542 8.056176  0.0000
soil         0.02662  0.199737 0.133289  0.8943

 Correlation: 
     (Intr)
soil -0.12 

Standardized residuals:
       Min         Q1        Med         Q3        Max 
-1.5811122 -0.7276873 -0.5028102 -0.2092991  0.3217326 

Residual standard error: 5.573087 
Degrees of freedom: 75 total; 73 residual


The range parameter is the distance scale of the exponential decay (correlation = exp(-distance / range)). Note the huge range here (about 700, larger than the study area): without a trend term, the correlation structure absorbs the large-scale trend, and the soil effect changes accordingly. This is only to show the syntax; in a real analysis, de-trend first.
Second, for glmmTMB. Here, we again have to prepare the data first

thickness$pos <- numFactor(thickness$east, 
                           thickness$north)
thickness$group <- factor(rep(1, nrow(thickness)))

fit3 = glmmTMB(thick ~ soil + exp(pos + 0 | group) , data = thickness)

The output of summary is a bit chunky, which is why I suppress it here

summary(fit3)

If you wonder why there is such a large correlation matrix displayed: both the AR1 and the exp(pos + 0 | group) structure impose a particular correlation structure on the random effects. Per default, glmmTMB shows correlations of random effects if they are estimated. In the case of the AR1 structure, the programmers apparently suppressed this, and just showed the estimate of the AR1 parameter. Here, however, they didn’t implement this feature, so you see the entire correlation structure, which is, admittedly, less helpful and should be changed.

11.3.1 Exercise — Does agriculture influence plant species richness?






CautionExercise — Plant counts in Regensburg



Use the dataset EcoData::plantcounts. Our scientific question is if richness ~ agrarea. Help on the dataset, as well as a few initial plots, is in the help of ?plantcounts.
This is count data, so start with a Poisson or Neg Binom GLM. The quadrats are not all equally sized, so you should include an offset to account for area (see ‘Log offset’ in Section 9.2.1.1). Then, check for spatial autocorrelation.
If you find autocorrelation that cannot be removed with a gam, the problem is that the gls function that we have used so far (Section 10.1.2, Section 11.2) only extends lm, and not glm models. In this case, you can either read up in https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/glmmTMB/vignettes/covstruct.html how to specify a spatial covariance in glmmTMB, or just log transform your counts + 1, and fit a gls (acceptable for large counts such as these, not for small counts with zeros).

title: 11  Correlation structures
text:
11.4 Phylogenetic structures (PGLS)



Closely related species share evolutionary history, so their trait values are not independent. Under Brownian motion, the covariance of two species is proportional to the length of the branch they share (vcv(tree)); a PGLS is simply a gls with this covariance structure, where the distance in the correlation structure is the phylogenetic distance. We fit with method = "ML" so that models with different fixed effects or correlation structures can be compared by AIC / LRT (Section 4.2.4).
This section is mostly taken from https://lukejharmon.github.io/ilhabela/instruction/2015/07/03/PGLS/. The two datasets associated with this example are in the EcoData package.
Perform analysis:

library(EcoData)
library(ape)
library(geiger)
library(nlme)
library(phytools)
library(DHARMa)

To plot the phylogenetic tree, use

plot(anolisTree)

Regress species traits

An old-school method to deal with the problem are the so-called Phylogenetically Independent Contrasts (PICs) (Felsenstein, 1985). The idea here is to transform your data in a way that an lm is still appropriate. For completeness, I show the method here.

Here, \(\lambda\) is estimated to be about 1, i.e. a strong phylogenetic signal, consistent with the Brownian motion model that we used in the PGLS.

title: 11  Correlation structures
text:
11.5 Take-home messages






Tip




Only the autocorrelation of the residuals matters, not that of the response or the predictors. Ignoring it makes p-values unreliable, so check the residuals of a model without a correlation structure (acf, variogram, DHARMa) to see whether you need one.
De-trend first (e.g. with a spline), and add a correlation structure only if autocorrelation remains. A correlation structure fitted on top of a misspecified trend absorbs the misfit and wrongly suggests a random correlation.
To check a fitted correlation structure, use the normalized residuals of gls (acf(residuals(fit, type = "normalized"))); DHARMa’s autocorrelation test is mainly useful for the model without correlation structure.
Phylogenetic correlation can make the p-values of an lm too small or too large. Check the residuals for phylogenetic signal and use a PGLS if there is some.
Do not interpret a model that has not converged; take warnings seriously and compare several starting values. Residual correlations between responses are not evidence of causal interactions.

title: 11  Correlation structures
text:
11.6 Multivariate GLMs



In recent years, multivariate GLMs, in particular the multivariate probit model, and latent variable versions thereof, have become popular for the analysis of community data. The keyword here is “joint species distribution models” (jSDMs).
Briefly, what we want a jSDM to do is to fit a vector of responses (could be abundance or presence / absence data) as a function of environmental predictors and a covariance between the responses. The model is thus
\[y \sim f(x) + \Sigma\] where y is a response vector, f(x) is a matrix with effects, and \(\Sigma\) is a covariance matrix that we want to estimate.
You can fit these models directly in lme4 or glmmTMB via implementing an RE per species

lme4::glmer(abundance ~ 0 + species + env:species + (0 + species | site), family = poisson, data = dat)
glmmTMB(abundance ~ 0 + species + env:species + (0 + species | site), family = poisson, data = dat)

however, these so-called full-rank models have a lot of degrees of freedom and are slow to compute if the number of species gets large. It has therefore become common to fit rank-reduced versions of these models using a latent-variable reparameterization of the model above. A latent-variable version of this model can be fit in glmmTMB via this syntax

glmmTMB(abundance ~ 0 + species + env:species + rr(0 + species | site, d = 2),
        family = poisson, data = dat)

The parameter d controls the number of latent variables. With d latent variables, all correlations between the responses are generated by d hidden gradients across the sampling units (here: sites), and each response has one loading per gradient; with small d, correlations close to ±1 therefore occur by construction.
Of course, there are many more specialized packages for fitting latent-variable jSDMs in R right now, including hmsc, gllvm or sjSDM, but I find it nice to place these models within the general topic of correlations, and to realize that we can fit them with the same methods and packages as all other correlation structures. The rr() structure in glmmTMB is described by McGillycuddy et al. (2025).

McGillycuddy, M. et al. (2025) “Parsimoniously fitting large multivariate random effects in glmmTMB,” Journal of Statistical Software, 112(1). Available at: https://doi.org/10.18637/jss.v112.i01.

11.6.1 Case study: cover of understory species
If a species has more cover than expected in a plot, do other species have more cover too, or less? Separate models for each species cannot answer this (Section 9.2.4.1). We use the varespec data from the plant cover case study in the GLM chapter (Section 9.7.2). To keep the model estimable with only 24 plots, we keep the 21 species that occur in at least 14 plots; the rarer half of the species is dropped, so all correlations refer to the common species. The cover is absolute (plot totals range from 64 to 126%), so a Dirichlet model does not apply. With 24 plots, this is a small data set: take the analysis as a demonstration, not a template.

library(vegan)
data(varespec)
data(varechem)
summary(rowSums(varespec))

   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  64.11   89.67  100.53  100.74  111.39  125.61 

keep <- names(which(colSums(varespec > 0) >= 14))
wide <- data.frame(site = factor(rownames(varespec)), varespec[, keep] / 100,
                   Al = scale(varechem$Al)[, 1], N = scale(varechem$N)[, 1])
long <- reshape(wide, direction = "long", varying = keep, v.names = "cover",
                timevar = "species", times = keep, idvar = "site")
long$species <- factor(long$species)

As a baseline, we fit an ordered beta model in which each species has its own intercept, its own response to aluminum and nitrogen, and its own precision (dispformula = ~ 0 + species, see Section 10.1.2; with a common precision for all species, the residual checks fail clearly). The plot effect (1 | site) accounts for plots with more or less vegetation overall. We use the ordered beta rather than the hurdle beta because the hurdle would double the number of parameters per species, too many for 24 plots.

ctl <- glmmTMBControl(optCtrl = list(iter.max = 2000, eval.max = 2000))
m_base <- glmmTMB(cover ~ 0 + species + species:Al + species:N + (1 | site),
                  dispformula = ~ 0 + species, family = ordbeta(),
                  data = long, control = ctl)
plot(simulateResiduals(m_base))

qu = 0.75, log(sigma) = -2.4794 : outer Newton did not converge fully.









Now we add two latent variables. The larger number of iterations (ctl) is needed for convergence:

m_rr <- update(m_base, . ~ . + rr(0 + species | site, d = 2))
m_rr$sdr$pdHess

[1] TRUE

m_rr$fit$message

[1] "relative convergence (4)"


Do the species co-vary beyond what the predictors and the plot effect (1 | site) explain? We compare the two models with AIC and BIC (Note 8.1):

ll <- sapply(list(m_base, m_rr), logLik)
k <- sapply(list(m_base, m_rr), function(m) attr(logLik(m), "df"))
data.frame(model = c("baseline", "baseline + rr(d = 2)"), df = k,
           AIC = -2 * ll + 2 * k,
           BIC_obs = -2 * ll + log(nrow(long)) * k,
           BIC_plots = -2 * ll + log(nlevels(long$site)) * k)

                 model  df       AIC   BIC_obs BIC_plots
1             baseline  87 -2745.017 -2377.653 -2642.526
2 baseline + rr(d = 2) 128 -2843.759 -2303.270 -2692.968


AIC clearly favors the joint model. BIC depends on what we count as \(n\): R uses the 504 observations (21 species × 24 plots), but the latent variables are estimated from only 24 plots. With \(n\) = 24, BIC agrees with AIC. We conclude that the species co-vary beyond the common plot effect. We use two latent variables because they can be displayed; more would improve AIC further, but 24 plots cannot support many more parameters.






TipChecking convergence





Latent-variable models often have several local optima, and optimizers can stop early. Refit the model from random starting values of the variance parameters (theta) and compare the log-likelihoods of the fits that converged:

set.seed(4)
nth <- length(m_rr$obj$env$parList()$theta)
sapply(1:6, function(i) {
  m <- update(m_rr, start = list(theta = rnorm(nth, 0, 0.5)))
  if (m$sdr$pdHess && m$fit$convergence == 0) as.numeric(logLik(m)) else NA
})

[1]      NA      NA 1549.88      NA      NA 1549.88

as.numeric(logLik(m_rr))

[1] 1549.88


Two of six starts reach the same optimum as our model; the others stop without convergence (NA). Rules: count a fit only if pdHess is TRUE and the message reports convergence; if converged fits reach different optima, take the best and be cautious; if none converge, reduce d or the number of species. Never interpret a model that has not converged.



We check the residuals by simulating new latent variables (simulateREs = "unconditional", see the explanation of conditional and unconditional simulations in Section 11.2), which checks the overall fit of the model:

plot(simulateResiduals(m_rr, simulateREs = "unconditional"))








Finally, the estimated correlations. In VarCorr(), site is the plot effect and site.1 the rr() term. For readability, we show only species with a latent standard deviation above 0.5:

S <- VarCorr(m_rr)$cond$site.1
dimnames(S) <- list(keep, keep)
round(sort(sqrt(diag(S)), decreasing = TRUE), 2)

Callvulg   Stersp Cetreric Cladunci Empenigr Cladrang Cladcris Vaccviti 
    2.79     1.72     1.32     1.02     0.88     0.65     0.57     0.56 
Dicrfusc Cladcocc Cladstel Cladcorn Pinusylv Cladarbu Claddefo Cladfimb 
    0.48     0.45     0.43     0.39     0.39     0.32     0.32     0.30 
Cladgrac Pleuschr Polyjuni Pohlnuta Ptilcili 
    0.18     0.18     0.14     0.13     0.10 

sel <- sqrt(diag(S)) > 0.5
heatmap(cov2cor(S[sel, sel]), symm = TRUE, scale = "none")








These are correlations of the latent plot effects on the logit scale, after removing the plot’s overall cover level; they are not correlations of the observed cover. Read them as groups of species that tend to have more (or less) cover in the same plots, not as single values. The fixed effects are now conditional on the latent variables, so some of them change compared with the baseline model (e.g. for Calluna).






ImportantResidual correlation is not a causal link



A residual correlation between two responses means that they are higher (or lower) in the same units than the predictors explain. This can be caused by unmeasured conditions of the units, by spatial structure (Section 11.3), or by a direct effect of one response on the other; the model cannot tell these apart. For species, this means that co-occurrence is not evidence of interactions (Blanchet, Cazelles and Gravel, 2020).



Blanchet, F.G., Cazelles, K. and Gravel, D. (2020) “Co-occurrence is not evidence of ecological interactions,” Ecology Letters, 23(7), pp. 1050–1063. Available at: https://doi.org/10.1111/ele.13525.






NoteCommunity data in practice



In ecology, data on many species are often analyzed with ordination (NMDS or PCoA with PERMANOVA, RDA, CCA), which describes the species composition as a whole but gives no model for single species. Model-based alternatives are mvabund::manyglm, gllvm (which also offers ordered and hurdle beta for cover data, as compared by Korhonen et al. (2024)), Hmsc (Bayesian) and sjSDM. If the hypothesis is about diversity, species richness may be the simpler response.





Korhonen, P. et al. (2024) “A comparison of joint species distribution models for percent cover data,” Methods in Ecology and Evolution, 15(12), pp. 2359–2372. Available at: https://doi.org/10.1111/2041-210X.14437.

title: 12  From question to paper: the analysis workflow
text:
12.1 The workflow at a glance
This chapter brings together what we have learned in this book as a workflow for analyzing your own data, from the scientific question to the methods and results sections of a paper. The seven steps are the same as in the overview at the beginning of the book (Section 1.1.2). Each step links to the sections where the respective topic is explained. If you have a concrete problem with your analysis, the table in the quick reference (Section B.1) points you to the relevant section.
crumbs: 12  From question to paper: the analysis workflow

title: 12  From question to paper: the analysis workflow
text:
Question and goal. Is your goal to estimate a causal effect, to predict, or to explore? The answer determines which variables you include and whether model selection is appropriate (Chapter 7, Chapter 8).
Design and data. What is the replicate (experimental unit), and how are the observations grouped (sites, plots, individuals, years)? Get an overview of the missing values (Chapter 6) and of the data: distribution of the response, range of and correlations between the predictors (Section 2.8). If you are still planning the study, see the section on design and power analysis (Section 12.7).
A-priori model. Choose the distribution from the type of response (Table 12.1), the predictors from the question (for causal questions with a causal diagram, Section 7.3), and the random effects and correlation structures from the design (Table 12.2). Center and scale numeric predictors if needed (Section 2.9). Specify this model before you look at the results.
Fit the model (Section 12.3).
Check the residuals and adjust the model (Table 12.3). Change the model to remove misfit, not to obtain significance (Section 8.2.4).
Inference: tests, confidence intervals, predictions (Section 12.4).
Report the analysis so that others can understand and reproduce it (Section 12.5).

12.2 From question to model



All models in this book are special cases of the general model shown in Section 1.1.1: a linear predictor (fixed effects, possibly with splines or nonlinear functions, plus random effects), a link function, a distribution and, if needed, a correlation structure. Building the a-priori model means choosing each of these components.
The distribution follows from the type of response:

The predictors follow from the goal of the analysis:

For a causal question, write down a causal diagram, adjust for confounders, but not for colliders, and for mediators only if you want the direct effect (Section 7.3). Only the effect of interest can be interpreted causally (Section 7.4.1).
For prediction, the goal is the model with the best out-of-sample performance, e.g. via AIC, cross-validation or shrinkage (Section 8.2, Section 8.4, Section 8.2.3).
An exploratory analysis can generate hypotheses, but its p-values are not valid tests of these hypotheses (Section 8.3.2).

The random effects and correlation structures follow from the design:

12.3 Fitting and checking the model
Packages to fit these models (see the quick reference in the appendix, Appendix B, for the syntax):

base R (stats): lm, glm.
lme4: mixed models, lmer, glmer.
mgcv: GAMs.
nlme: variance and correlation structures for linear (mixed) models, using gls and lme.
glmmTMB: generalized linear mixed models with variance and correlation structures and zero-inflation.

Alternatively, you could move to Bayesian estimates with brms, which can fit all of these models, makes it easier to include shrinkage, and makes p-value and degrees-of-freedom problems less visible (see the Bayesian workflow in Hartig (2024)).
Check the fitted model with residual plots, for GLMs and mixed models with the simulated residuals of DHARMa (Section 2.4.2, Section 9.3.1), and adjust the model if you find a problem. Work through the problems roughly in the order of the table: a wrong functional form or distribution can create apparent dispersion or correlation problems.



Table 12.3: Typical problems in residual checks and what to do about them.

Section 4.4.1






Note that since version 0.5.0, DHARMa simulates the residuals of mixed models conditional on the fitted random effects by default. To detect patterns at the level of the groups (e.g. spatial autocorrelation between sites), use simulateResiduals(..., simulateREs = "unconditional"). Note, however, that unconditional residuals of a model with a fitted correlation structure still contain the full autocorrelation, so they cannot show whether this structure is adequate (see the subsection on conditional residual checks in Section 11.2).

12.4 Inference
Once the model is final, you can test hypotheses and calculate confidence intervals. The main options:

Comparisons between groups

Remember that p-values and confidence intervals are only valid for hypotheses that were specified before looking at the data. After model selection, they are too optimistic (Section 8.3.2). For nonlinear link functions, report effects on the response scale (Caution 9.1), and for mixed models, decide whether you want conditional, unconditional or marginal predictions (Tip 4.3).

title: 12  From question to paper: the analysis workflow
text:
12.5 Reporting
The methods section should allow others to reproduce your analysis:

the question, and whether the analysis was planned in advance or exploratory;
the response, the distribution and link, and the model formula, including the reasons for the random effects;
the handling of missing values, transformations, centering and scaling;
which residual checks you did (e.g. DHARMa simulated residuals: uniformity, dispersion, zero-inflation), and how you adjusted the model;
how model selection was done, if any;
how p-values and confidence intervals were calculated (test type, e.g. Wald or likelihood ratio test, and CI method, e.g. profile or bootstrap; for mixed models also the estimation method, ML or REML);
the software and package versions (and citations, e.g. citation("glmmTMB")).

Closely related is the reproducibility of your analysis, which reviewers and journals increasingly expect:

Do the entire analysis in a script (or a Quarto / R Markdown document), from reading the raw data to the final figures, not in the console. Never change the raw data by hand; do all corrections in the script. Use relative paths (e.g. with an RStudio project), so that the script also runs on another computer.
Set a seed (set.seed()) at the top of the script and before each step that uses random numbers (simulations, bootstrap, simulated LRTs, cross-validation, imputation), so that you and others get the same results. DHARMa fixes its own seed by default (argument seed of simulateResiduals()), so its residuals are reproducible anyway.
Record the R and package versions with sessionInfo() (results can change between versions, even for the same seed). To reproduce them later, use the renv package (renv::init(), renv::snapshot() to write the versions to renv.lock, renv::restore() to reinstall them).
Deposit the data (with a short description of all columns), the code and the renv.lock file together with the paper, e.g. on Zenodo or Dryad, and cite the DOI in a data and code availability statement.

The results section should report effect sizes with confidence intervals, on an interpretable scale, together with the number of observations and groups, and, where appropriate, effect plots with confidence intervals (Section 2.3). For GLMs, the coefficients are on the scale of the link function, so they should be translated (Table 12.5):



Table 12.5: How to report coefficients for different link functions.










Link

What to report

logit (binomial)
the odds are multiplied by \(e^\beta\) per unit of x
odds ratio \(e^\beta\) with CI

predicted means with CIs, e.g. emmeans(fit, ~ x, type = "response"); for mixed models, say whether these are unconditional (random effects at zero) or marginal predictions (Tip 4.3)






For example, for the number of warp breaks in a weaving experiment (negative binomial GLM), the effects as rate ratios with CIs and the predicted means per tension level are:

library(MASS)
library(emmeans)
fit = glm.nb(breaks ~ tension + wool, data = warpbreaks)
exp(cbind(estimate = coef(fit), confint(fit))) # rate ratios with 95% CI

              estimate      2.5 %     97.5 %
(Intercept) 39.3838001 32.7556034 47.6129920
tensionM     0.7413909  0.5832160  0.9423597
tensionH     0.5996582  0.4704206  0.7641473
woolB        0.8300984  0.6803374  1.0127898

 L           35.9 3.03 Inf      30.4      42.3

Results are averaged over the levels of: wool 
Confidence level used: 0.95 
Intervals are back-transformed from the log scale 


A results sentence could then read: “Compared to low tension, the number of breaks was 26% lower at medium tension (rate ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.58-0.94) and 40% lower at high tension (0.60, 0.47-0.76; negative binomial GLM, n = 54, wool type held constant, profile-likelihood CIs).” For a mixed model, also state the number of observations and groups per random effect and the estimated random effect standard deviations (VarCorr()), e.g. “480 observations from 24 sites; standard deviation between sites 0.4 on the log scale”. For a numeric predictor, calculate predictions with predict(..., se.fit = TRUE) on the link scale, add ± 1.96 standard errors, back-transform with the inverse link (e.g. exp() for the log link), and plot them together with the data (Section 2.11; for mixed models, Section 4.5.2). An example of a methods and results text for an ANOVA is in Section 3.2.4.3.






CautionCommon mistakes in reporting




reporting p-values without effect sizes and confidence intervals;
reading a non-significant result as “no effect” (look at the confidence interval instead);
concluding that an effect differs between groups because it is significant in one group but not in the other, instead of testing the difference (Note 3.1);
interpreting GLM coefficients as if they were on the response scale;
reporting a model found by model selection as if it had been planned in advance (Section 8.3.2);
using causal language for a predictive or exploratory analysis (Chapter 7).

title: 12  From question to paper: the analysis workflow
text:
12.6 Thoughts about the analysis pipeline



In statistics, we rarely use a simple analysis. We often use an entire pipeline, consisting, for example, of the workflow sketched in Section 12.1. What we should constantly ask ourselves: Is our pipeline good? By “good”, we typically mean: If 1000 analyses are run in that way:

What is the typical error of the estimate?
What is the Type I error (false positives)?
Are the confidence intervals correctly calculated?
…

The way to check this is to run simulations. For example, the following function creates data that follows the assumptions of a linear regression with slope 0.5, then fits a linear regression, and returns the estimate

getEstimate = function(n = 100){
  x = runif(n)
  y = 0.5 * x + rnorm(n)
  fit = lm(y ~ x)
  x = summary(fit)
  return(x$coefficients[2, 1])  # Get fitted x weight (should be ~0.5).
}

The replicate function allows us to execute this 1000 times:

set.seed(543210)

out = replicate(1000, getEstimate())

Plotting the result, we can check whether the linear regression is an unbiased estimator for the slope.

hist(out, breaks = 50)
abline(v = 0.5, col = "red")








“Unbiased” means that, while each single estimate has some error, the errors average out: the mean of many estimates is the true value (up to simulation error).
Explicitly calculating these values
Bias

mean(out) - 0.5 # Should be ~0.

[1] -0.001826401


Variance / standard deviation of the estimator

sd(out)

[1] 0.3587717


To check p-values, we could run:

set.seed(12345)

getEstimate = function(n = 100){  # Mind: Function has changed!
  x = runif(n)
  y = rnorm(n)  # No dependence of x! Identical: y = 0 * x + rnorm(n).
  fit = lm(y ~ x)
  x = summary(fit)
  return(x$coefficients[2, 4])  # P-value for H0: Weight of x = 0.
}

out = replicate(2000, getEstimate())

hist(out) # Expected: Uniformly distributed p-values. -> Check.







mean(out < 0.05) # Type I error rate: fraction of p-values < 0.05 when H0 is true; about 0.05 for a calibrated test

[1] 0.0515

# Explanation of syntax: Logical vectors are interpreted as vectors of 0s and 1s.

To check the properties of other, possibly more complicated pipelines, statisticians will typically use the same technique. I recommend doing this! For example, you could modify the function above to have a non-normal error. How much difference does that make? Simulating often beats recommendations in the books!

title: 12  From question to paper: the analysis workflow
text:
12.7 Experimental design and power analysis



All we have learned in this course directly informs experimental and research design, be it controlled experiments, quasi-experiments or observational studies.
As a start, note our discussions of causality (Chapter 7) and model selection (Chapter 8):

First of all, research design needs a goal: do you want to design for prediction or (causal) inference
If you are after causal inference, randomize or hold constant what you can; measure what you cannot control so that you can adjust for it. It is often possible even in observational settings to control confounders, e.g. by selecting the observations in a way that confounders are at the same value. This can be useful because, as we discussed in the section on collinearity (Section 2.8), adjusting for collinear variables is possible, but costs power.
In experimental settings, blocked designs where blocks will be later treated as a random effect (see Chapter 4) are standard

If you have decided on the selection of variables, treat your analysis as fixed. Perform a pilot study and/or a power analysis for the entire study.
The cleanest way to do a power analysis for any model - not just the textbook cases - is by simulation: assume an effect size, simulate many datasets, fit your planned model to each, and count how often the effect comes out significant. That fraction is the power.

getP = function(n = 50, effect = 1){
  x = runif(n)
  y = effect * x + rnorm(n)          # assumed true effect + noise
  summary(lm(y ~ x))$coefficients[2, 4]
}

mean(replicate(1000, getP(n = 50, effect = 1)) < 0.05)   # power at n = 50 (about 0.5)

[1] 0.507


To find the sample size for, say, 80% power, wrap this in a loop over n (here, roughly 100 observations are needed). Note that the assumed effect should be the smallest biologically relevant effect (or a plausible one from the literature), not the effect observed in the data: power calculated from an observed effect is uninformative. The same recipe works for GLMMs, spatial models, etc. - just swap the data-generating step and the fitted model, which is why simulation beats closed-form power formulas once you leave the simple LM.

title: 12  From question to paper: the analysis workflow
text:
12.8 Next steps



This book covered the core GLMM toolbox. Natural next steps are the fully Bayesian treatment of these models (brms / Stan), which sidesteps several of the degrees-of-freedom and p-value problems we flagged along the way, and hierarchical models such as error-in-variable, occupancy and state-space models (all covered in Hartig (2024)); machine-learning approaches when the goal is purely prediction; and domain-specific extensions such as joint species distribution models, survival / time-to-event models, and structural equation models - each of which builds directly on the ideas developed here.



Hartig, F. (2024) “Introduction to Bayesian statistics with R.” Available at: https://florianhartig.github.io/LearningBayes/.

B.6 Correlation structures
Correlation structures are explained in Chapter 11 (temporal: Section 11.2, spatial: Section 11.3, phylogenetic: Section 11.4).

B.6.1 glmmTMB
glmmTMB supports several correlation structures; the following table shows two common ones. See also the glmmTMB vignette about correlation structures.



Table B.6: Correlation structures in glmmTMB.











Type
Code
Interpretation
Section




Spatial
data$coords = numFactor(data$x, data$y); data$group = factor(1); glmmTMB(y ~ x + exp(0 + coords | group), data = data)
random intercepts per location with exponentially decaying covariance (geostatistical); group = factor(1) if there is one spatial field
Section 11.3


Temporal
data$yearF = factor(data$year); glmmTMB(y ~ x + ar1(0 + yearF | group), data = data)
random intercepts per time point (time must be a factor) with AR(1) correlation within each group; group is required, use data$group = factor(1) for a single time series
Section 11.2








B.6.2 lme4
lme4 has no correlation structures for residuals (use glmmTMB, or nlme for linear models).

Type
Formula
Interpretation

text:
C.1 Hurricanes
General strategy for analysis (see also the workflow in Chapter 12):
Fit this base model, then do residual checks for
And adjust the model accordingly.
In Jung et al. (2014), the authors claim that “Female hurricanes are deadlier than male hurricanes”.
Specifically, they analyze the number of hurricane fatalities, and claim that there is an effect of the femininity of the name on the number of fatalities, correcting for several possible confounders. They interpret the result as causal (including mediators), claiming that giving only male names to hurricanes would considerably reduce death toll.
The data is available in DHARMa.
library(DHARMa)
library(mgcv)

CautionTasks




Confirm that you get the same results as in the paper. It makes sense to translate their model to glmmTMB. Note that the nb parameterization of mgcv corresponds to nbinom2 in glmmTMB. You will get different results when choosing nbinom1
Inspect the fitted model for potential problems, in particular perform a residual analysis of the model, including residuals against all predictors, and improve the model if you find problems.
Forget what they did. Go back to start, do a causal analysis like we did (Chapter 7), and do your own model, diagnosing all residual problems that we discussed (Section 2.4, Section 9.3, Chapter 10, Chapter 11). Do you think there is an effect of femininity?









TipSolution





This is the model fit by Jung et al. (2014), fit with glmmTMB

library(DHARMa)
library(glmmTMB)

m1 = glmmTMB(alldeaths ~ MasFem*
                             (Minpressure_Updated_2014 + scale(NDAM)),
                           data = hurricanes, family = nbinom2)
summary(m1)

 Family: nbinom2  ( log )
Formula:          alldeaths ~ MasFem * (Minpressure_Updated_2014 + scale(NDAM))
Data: hurricanes

      AIC       BIC    logLik -2*log(L)  df.resid 
    660.7     678.4    -323.4     646.7        85 


Dispersion parameter for nbinom2 family (): 0.787 

Conditional model:
                                 Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)                     69.661590  23.425598   2.974 0.002942 ** 
MasFem                          -5.855078   2.716589  -2.155 0.031138 *  
Minpressure_Updated_2014        -0.069870   0.024251  -2.881 0.003964 ** 
scale(NDAM)                     -0.494094   0.455968  -1.084 0.278536    
MasFem:Minpressure_Updated_2014  0.006108   0.002813   2.171 0.029901 *  
MasFem:scale(NDAM)               0.205418   0.061956   3.316 0.000915 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Note that the model above scales only NDAM (and the paper does not say whether they scaled), but as we are looking for main effects in the presence of interactions, we should definitely scale to improve the interpretability (see Section 2.10.3)

m2 = glmmTMB(alldeaths ~ scale(MasFem) *
                             (scale(Minpressure_Updated_2014) + scale(NDAM)),
                           data = hurricanes, family = nbinom2)
summary(m2)

 Family: nbinom2  ( log )
Formula:          
alldeaths ~ scale(MasFem) * (scale(Minpressure_Updated_2014) +  
    scale(NDAM))
Data: hurricanes

      AIC       BIC    logLik -2*log(L)  df.resid 
    660.7     678.4    -323.4     646.7        85 


Dispersion parameter for nbinom2 family (): 0.787 

Conditional model:
                                              Estimate Std. Error z value
(Intercept)                                     2.5034     0.1231  20.341
scale(MasFem)                                   0.1237     0.1210   1.022
scale(Minpressure_Updated_2014)                -0.5425     0.1603  -3.384
scale(NDAM)                                     0.8988     0.2190   4.105
scale(MasFem):scale(Minpressure_Updated_2014)   0.3758     0.1731   2.171
scale(MasFem):scale(NDAM)                       0.6629     0.1999   3.316
                                              Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)                                    < 2e-16 ***
scale(MasFem)                                 0.306923    
scale(Minpressure_Updated_2014)               0.000715 ***
scale(NDAM)                                   4.05e-05 ***
scale(MasFem):scale(Minpressure_Updated_2014) 0.029901 *  
scale(MasFem):scale(NDAM)                     0.000915 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


now main effect is n.s.; it’s a bit dodgy, but if you read in the main paper, they do not claim a significant main effect, they mainly argue via ANOVA and significance at high values of NDAM, so let’s run an ANOVA. car::Anova() gives type II tests, which, unlike type III, do not depend on the centering (see Section 3.2.4 and Caution 3.1):

car::Anova(m2)

Analysis of Deviance Table (Type II Wald chisquare tests)

Response: alldeaths
                                                Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq)    
scale(MasFem)                                  1.9495  1  0.1626364    
scale(Minpressure_Updated_2014)                7.1285  1  0.0075868 ** 
scale(NDAM)                                   14.6100  1  0.0001322 ***
scale(MasFem):scale(Minpressure_Updated_2014)  4.7150  1  0.0299011 *  
scale(MasFem):scale(NDAM)                     10.9929  1  0.0009146 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


In the ANOVA we see that MasFem still n.s. but interactions, and if you would calculate effect of MasFem at high NDAM, it is significant. Something like that is argued in the paper. We can emulate this by changing NDAM centering to high NDAM, which gives us a p-value for the main effect of MasFem at high values of NDAM

hurricanes$highcenteredNDAM = hurricanes$NDAM - max(hurricanes$NDAM)

m3 = glmmTMB(alldeaths ~ scale(MasFem) *
                             (scale(Minpressure_Updated_2014) + highcenteredNDAM),
                           data = hurricanes, family = nbinom2)
summary(m3)

 Family: nbinom2  ( log )
Formula:          
alldeaths ~ scale(MasFem) * (scale(Minpressure_Updated_2014) +  
    highcenteredNDAM)
Data: hurricanes

      AIC       BIC    logLik -2*log(L)  df.resid 
    660.7     678.4    -323.4     646.7        85 


Dispersion parameter for nbinom2 family (): 0.787 

Conditional model:
                                                Estimate Std. Error z value
(Intercept)                                    7.210e+00  1.149e+00   6.275
scale(MasFem)                                  3.595e+00  1.041e+00   3.455
scale(Minpressure_Updated_2014)               -5.425e-01  1.603e-01  -3.384
highcenteredNDAM                               6.949e-05  1.693e-05   4.105
scale(MasFem):scale(Minpressure_Updated_2014)  3.758e-01  1.731e-01   2.171
scale(MasFem):highcenteredNDAM                 5.125e-05  1.546e-05   3.316
                                              Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)                                   3.50e-10 ***
scale(MasFem)                                 0.000551 ***
scale(Minpressure_Updated_2014)               0.000715 ***
highcenteredNDAM                              4.05e-05 ***
scale(MasFem):scale(Minpressure_Updated_2014) 0.029904 *  
scale(MasFem):highcenteredNDAM                0.000915 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


Now we see the significant main effect that they report. Note, however, that the significant difference is only there for high NDAM, i.e. what we do here is to project the effect of the interaction on the main effect. An alternative to do the same thing would be an effects plot (Section 2.3), or to specifically use predict() (Section 2.11) to calculate differences and CIs at high NDAM values.

library(effects)
plot(allEffects(m3, partial.residuals = T))








OK, this means we can replicate the results of the paper, even if concentrating the entire analysis exclusive on high NDAM seems a bit cherry-picking. Choosing the evaluation point after looking at the data inflates the false-positive risk, and at the maximum NDAM the estimate rests on very few storms. Another way to phrase the result is that we don’t find a main effect of MasFem. However, to be fair: the current results do say that there is a significant difference at high NDAM, and such a difference, if it existed, would be important.
But we haven’t done residual checks yet. Let’s do that:

res <- simulateResiduals(originalModelGAM)
plot(res)







plotResiduals(res, hurricanes$NDAM)







plotResiduals(res, hurricanes$MasFem)







plotResiduals(res, hurricanes$Minpressure_Updated_2014)








No significant deviation in the general DHARMa plot, but residuals ~ NDAM looks funny, which was also pointed out by Bob O’Hara in a blog post after publication of the paper. Let’s try to correct this - transforming NDAM with ^0.2 (found by trying a few powers; 0.1 to 0.2 fit best) does a great job:

correctedModel = glmmTMB(alldeaths ~ scale(MasFem) *
                             (scale(Minpressure_Updated_2014) + scale(NDAM^0.2)),
                          data = hurricanes, family = nbinom2)

res <- simulateResiduals(correctedModel, plot = T)







plotResiduals(res, hurricanes$NDAM)







summary(correctedModel)

 Family: nbinom2  ( log )
Formula:          
alldeaths ~ scale(MasFem) * (scale(Minpressure_Updated_2014) +  
    scale(NDAM^0.2))
Data: hurricanes

      AIC       BIC    logLik -2*log(L)  df.resid 
    630.8     648.5    -308.4     616.8        85 


Dispersion parameter for nbinom2 family (): 1.11 

Conditional model:
                                              Estimate Std. Error z value
(Intercept)                                    2.26430    0.10912  20.751
scale(MasFem)                                  0.05156    0.10695   0.482
scale(Minpressure_Updated_2014)               -0.03162    0.18141  -0.174

                                              Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)                                    < 2e-16 ***
scale(MasFem)                                    0.630    
scale(Minpressure_Updated_2014)                  0.862    
scale(NDAM^0.2)                               1.12e-11 ***

---

Analysis of Deviance Table (Type II Wald chisquare tests)

Response: alldeaths
                                                Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq)    
scale(MasFem)                                  0.5732  1     0.4490    
scale(Minpressure_Updated_2014)                0.1255  1     0.7232    
scale(NDAM^0.2)                               73.5010  1     <2e-16 ***
scale(MasFem):scale(Minpressure_Updated_2014)  0.0140  1     0.9057    
scale(MasFem):scale(NDAM^0.2)                  0.6216  1     0.4304    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


All gone, only damage is doing the effect. This wouldn’t change with re-scaling probably, as interactions are n.s.
What if we would have fit our own model? First of all, note that if hurricane names were given randomly, we wouldn’t have to worry about confounders (Section 7.2.1). However, this is not the case, hurricanes were only named randomly after 1978 or so.

plot(MasFem ~ Year, data = hurricanes)








So, we could either take the earlier data out, which would remove half of our data, or we have to worry about confounding with variables that change over time. The most obvious thing would be to take time itself (Year) in the model, to correct for temporal confounding.
Do we need other variables that are not confounders? There are two reasons to add them (the first is the idea of precision variables, Tip 8.1):

they have strong effects on the response - not adding them could lead to residual problems and increase residual variance, which increases uncertainties and cost power
we want to fit interactions.

I added NDAM to the model, because we saw earlier that it has a strong effect. I think it’s not unreasonable to check for an interaction as well.
As we have several observations per year, a conservative approach would be to add a RE on year. Note that we use year both as a fixed effect (to remove temporal trends) and a random intercept, which is perfectly fine, however.

newModel = glmmTMB(alldeaths ~ scale(MasFem) * scale(NDAM^0.2) + Year + (1|Year),
                           data = hurricanes, family = nbinom2)
summary(newModel)

 Family: nbinom2  ( log )
Formula:          
alldeaths ~ scale(MasFem) * scale(NDAM^0.2) + Year + (1 | Year)
Data: hurricanes

      AIC       BIC    logLik -2*log(L)  df.resid 
    630.8     648.4    -308.4     616.8        85 

Random effects:

Conditional model:
 Groups Name        Variance  Std.Dev. 
 Year   (Intercept) 2.571e-07 0.0005071
Number of obs: 92, groups:  Year, 49

Dispersion parameter for nbinom2 family (): 1.11 

Conditional model:
                               Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)                   -2.542287  12.730846  -0.200    0.842    
scale(MasFem)                  0.073207   0.119273   0.614    0.539    
scale(NDAM^0.2)                1.309624   0.118106  11.089   <2e-16 ***
Year                           0.002426   0.006423   0.378    0.706    
scale(MasFem):scale(NDAM^0.2)  0.179874   0.117191   1.535    0.125    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

car::Anova(newModel) # nothing regarding MasFem

Analysis of Deviance Table (Type II Wald chisquare tests)

Response: alldeaths
                                 Chisq Df Pr(>Chisq)    
scale(MasFem)                   0.5563  1     0.4558    
scale(NDAM^0.2)               121.9237  1     <2e-16 ***
Year                            0.1426  1     0.7057    
scale(MasFem):scale(NDAM^0.2)   2.3559  1     0.1248    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1


The variance of the year random effect is estimated as practically zero (a boundary fit), so there is no extra year-to-year variation beyond the fixed effect of Year, and removing the random effect would not change the results. The results remain that there is no effect of MasFem!




Jung, K. et al. (2014) “Female hurricanes are deadlier than male hurricanes,” Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 111(24), pp. 8782–8787. Available at: https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1402786111.

title: Appendix C — Case studies
section: C.2 Researcher degrees of freedom — skin color and red cards
text:
C.2 Researcher degrees of freedom — skin color and red cards



Silberzahn et al. (2018) published a “meta-analysis” in Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, where they had provided 29 teams with the same data set to answer one research question: “[W]hether soccer players with dark skin tone are more likely than those with light skin tone to receive red cards from referees”.
Spoiler: They found that the “[a]nalytic approaches varied widely across the teams, and the estimated effect sizes ranged from 0.89 to 2.93 (Mdn = 1.31) in odds-ratio units”, highlighting that different approaches in data analysis can yield significant variation in the results.
The data is in

library(EcoData)
?redCards







CautionTasks



Do a re-analysis of the data as if you were the 30th team to contribute the results to the meta-analysis. You can find the data in the ecodata package, dataset redCards.

Response variable: ‘redCards’ (+‘yellowReds’?).
primary predictors: ‘rater1’, ‘rater2’
Multiple variables, potentially accounting for confounding, offsetting, grouping, … are included in the data.



The rater variable contains ratings of “two independent raters blind to the research question who, based on their profile photo, categorized players on a 5-point scale ranging from (1) very light skin to (5) very dark skin. Note that ‘rater1’ and ‘rater2’ in EcoData::redCards are already rescaled to the range 0 … 1, as described in the paper (”This variable was rescaled to be bounded by 0 (very light skin) and 1 (very dark skin) prior to the final analysis, to ensure consistency of effect sizes across the teams of analysts. The raw ratings were rescaled to 0, .25, .50, .75, and 1 to create this new scale.”)
When you’re done, have a look at the other modeling teams. Do you understand the models they fit? Note that the results are displayed in terms of odds ratios. Are your results within the range of estimates from the 29 teams in Silberzahn et al. (2018)?






TipSolution





Base model
There is no single “correct” analysis - that is the whole point of Silberzahn et al. (2018). The following is therefore not a fully worked-out solution, but one defensible base model to start from. Each row is a player-referee dyad, so red cards are a count out of the number of games the two shared; we use that as exposure via a log offset, take the mean of the two skin-tone ratings rescaled to 0-1 as the predictor, and add random effects for player and referee to respect the non-independence.

library(EcoData); library(glmmTMB); library(DHARMa)
d = redCards
d$skin  = (d$rater1 + d$rater2)/2     # mean of the two ratings (already on the 0..1 scale)
d = d[!is.na(d$skin) & d$games > 0, ]

m = glmmTMB(redCards ~ skin + (1|playerShort) + (1|refNum),
            offset = log(games), family = poisson, data = d)
summary(m)

 Family: poisson  ( log )
Formula:          redCards ~ skin + (1 | playerShort) + (1 | refNum)
Data: d
 Offset: log(games)

      AIC       BIC    logLik -2*log(L)  df.resid 
  15543.6   15582.5   -7767.8   15535.6    124617 

Random effects:

Conditional model:
 Groups      Name        Variance Std.Dev.
 playerShort (Intercept) 0.3659   0.6049  
 refNum      (Intercept) 0.1481   0.3849  
Number of obs: 124621, groups:  playerShort, 1585; refNum, 2978

Conditional model:
            Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept) -5.78507    0.05547  -104.3  < 2e-16 ***
skin         0.32961    0.10649     3.1  0.00197 ** 
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

exp(fixef(m)$cond["skin"])   # rate ratio, darkest (1) vs lightest (0) skin

    skin 
1.390424 

res = simulateResiduals(m); plot(res); testDispersion(res)
















    DHARMa nonparametric dispersion test via sd of residuals fitted vs.
    simulated

data:  simulationOutput
dispersion = 1.0768, p-value = 0.008
alternative hypothesis: two.sided


The exponentiated skin coefficient is our effect in rate-ratio units (comparable to the paper’s odds ratios: red cards are rare, about 0.4% per player-referee game, and for rare events a rate ratio is close to an odds ratio). Compare it to the 0.89-2.93 range of odds ratios reported across the 29 teams. This bare model gives a rate ratio of about 1.4, which is inside the range of the 29 teams and close to their median (1.31). The study shows, however, that the “researcher degrees of freedom” (choice of exposure, random-effect structure, which rater, count vs. binomial, and - crucially - which confounders are included) can move the result substantially. From this base model, you would go on to address the slight overdispersion (Section 9.3) and to add plausible confounders (see Chapter 7; league, playing position, player skill, …) and see how much the estimate changes.




Silberzahn, R. et al. (2018) “Many analysts, one data set: Making transparent how variations in analytic choices affect results,” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), pp. 337–356. Available at: https://doi.org/10.1177/2515245917747646.

title: Appendix C — Case studies
text:
C.3 Scouting ants









CautionTasks



Look at the dataset EcoData::scoutingAnts, and find out if there are really scouting ants in Lasius niger.


A base model should be:

library(EcoData)
dat = scoutingAnts[scoutingAnts$first.visit == 0,]
dat$ant_group = as.factor(dat$ant_group)
dat$ant_group_main = as.factor(dat$ant_group_main)

fit <- glm(went.phero ~ ant_group_main, data = dat, family = binomial)
summary(fit)


Call:
glm(formula = went.phero ~ ant_group_main, family = binomial, 
    data = dat)

Coefficients:
                                       Estimate Std. Error z value Pr(>|z|)    
(Intercept)                             0.67398    0.09775   6.895 5.39e-12 ***
ant_group_mainSecondvisit_1st_to_phero  0.16690    0.11371   1.468    0.142    
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

(Dispersion parameter for binomial family taken to be 1)

    Null deviance: 2322.8  on 1874  degrees of freedom
Residual deviance: 2320.7  on 1873  degrees of freedom
AIC: 2324.7

Number of Fisher Scoring iterations: 4








TipSolution





For me, it made sense to change the contrasts of the possible confounders (see Section 2.6.1) into something more easily interpretable:

Did the side in which the pheromone was stay constant or not (testing for a directional persistence of the ants)
Was the pheromone in the left or the right arm (testing for a directional preference)


dat$directionConst = ifelse(dat$Treatment %in% c("LL", "RR"), T, F)
dat$directionPhero = as.factor(ifelse(dat$Treatment %in% c("LL", "RL"), "left", "right"))

Together with the orientation of the Maze, this makes 3 possible directional confounders, and the main predictor (if the Ant went to the pheromone in the first visit).
Adding an RE on colony is logical, and then let’s run the model:

library(lme4)
fit1<-glmer(went.phero ~ ant_group_main
             + directionConst
             + directionPhero
             + Orientation
             + (1|Colony),family="binomial", 
             data=dat)
summary(fit1)

an__S_1__:O  0.225 -0.526     0.089  0.034 -0.845 -0.021      0.046    


We now find that there is an interaction with the main predictor, and there could be effects. We can also look at this visually.

plot(allEffects(fit2))








The results are difficult to interpret. I would think that there was some bias in the experiment, which led to an effect of the Maze direction, which then creates a spill-over to the other (and in particular the main) predictors.
For our education, we can also look at the residual plots. I will use fit1, because there was a misfit:

res <- simulateResiduals(fit1, plot = T)








As we would expect significant interactions, we would probably see something if we plot residuals against predictors or their interactions, but I want to show you something else:
We will not see dispersion problems in a 0/1 binomial, but actually, this is a k/n binomial, just that the data are not prepared as such.
Either way, in DHARMa, you can aggregate residuals by a grouping variable.

res2 <- recalculateResiduals(res, group = dat$Colony)

Now, we essentially check k/n data, and we see that there is overdispersion, which is caused by the misfit.

plot(res2)







testDispersion(res2)









    DHARMa nonparametric dispersion test via sd of residuals fitted vs.
    simulated

data:  simulationOutput
dispersion = 1.0233, p-value = 0.832
alternative hypothesis: two.sided


Let’s do the same for model 2, which included the interactions.

res <- simulateResiduals(fit2, plot = T)







res2 <- recalculateResiduals(res, group = dat$Colony)

plot(res2)

Warning in newton(lsp = lsp, X = G$X, y = G$y, Eb = G$Eb, UrS = G$UrS, L = G$L,
: Fitting terminated with step failure - check results carefully








testDispersion(res2)









    DHARMa nonparametric dispersion test via sd of residuals fitted vs.
    simulated

data:  simulationOutput
dispersion = 1.0422, p-value = 0.736
alternative hypothesis: two.sided


Which largely removes the problem!

title: Appendix C — Case studies
text:
C.4 Snails




library(EcoData)
library(glmmTMB)
library(lme4)
library(DHARMa)
?EcoData::snails

Look at the Snails data set in the EcoData package, and find out which environmental and/or seasonal predictors i) explain the total abundance and ii) the infection rate of Bulinus spp.
The snails data set in the EcoData package includes observations on the distribution of freshwater snails and their infection rates ( schistosomiasis (a parasite)).
The first scientific question is that their abundance depends on the water conditions. The second scientific question is that their infection rate depends on the water conditions and seasonal factors
The data also contains data on other environmental (and seasonal factors). You should consider if it is useful to add them to the analysis.
Species: BP_tot (Biomphalaria pfeifferi), BF_tot (Bulinus forskalii), BT_tot (Bulinus truncatus)
Number of infected individuals: BP_pos_tot, BF_pos_tot, BT_pos_tot
Total abundance of Bulinus spp.: Bulinus_tot
Total number of infected Bulinus spp.: Bulinus_pos_tot






CautionTasks




Model the total abundance of Bulinus spp. (Bulinus_tot)
Model the infection rate of Bulinus spp. (Bulinus_pos_tot) (k/n binomial)
Optional: Model the species individually (BP_tot, BF_tot, BT_tot)
Optional: Fit a multivariate (joint) species distribution model (see Section 11.6)

library(glmmTMB)
library(DHARMa)

data$swater_depth = scale(data$water_depth)

data = data[rows, ]

Prevalence of Bulinus (GLMM)
Prepare+scale data:

library(lme4)
library(glmmTMB)
library(DHARMa)
data = EcoData::snails
data$sTemp_Water = scale(data$Temp_Water)
data$spH = scale(data$pH)
data$swater_speed_ms = scale(data$water_speed_ms)
data$swater_depth = scale(data$water_depth)
data$sCond = scale(data$Cond)
data$swmo_prec = scale(data$wmo_prec)
data$syear = scale(data$year)
data$sLat = scale(data$Latitude)
data$sLon = scale(data$Longitude)
data$sTemp_Air = scale(data$Temp_Air)

# Remove NAs beforehand: model.matrix drops only the rows with an NA in a variable used in the model
# (complete.cases(data) would also drop rows with NAs in unused columns); all models then use the same rows:
rows = rownames(model.matrix(Bulinus_tot~sTemp_Water + spH + sLat + sLon + sCond + seas_wmo+ swmo_prec + swater_speed_ms + swater_depth +sTemp_Air+ syear + duration + locality + site_irn + coll_date, data = data))
data = data[rows, ]

Let’s start directly with all potential confounders (see previous solution):

Multivariate (joint) species distribution model
The species models are connected by their response to latent variable (unobserved environment). For that, we will transform our dataset with respect to species from wide (sp1, sp2, sp3) to long format (species abundances in one column and a second column telling us the group (species)). In the model then, we will separate the species and their responses by using ~0+Species + Species:(predictors).
The latent variable structure is set by the rr(…) object in the formula:

C.5 Seed bank




library(EcoData)
library(glmmTMB)
library(lme4)
library(lmerTest)
library(DHARMa)
?EcoData::seedBank

The seedBank data set in the EcoData package includes observation on seed bank presence and size in different vegetation plots.
The scientific question is if the ability of plants to build a seed bank depends on their seed traits (see help).
The data also contains data on environmental factors and plant traits. You should consider if it is useful to add them to the analysis.

#the following code was taken from https://github.com/glmmTMB/glmmTMB/blob/master/misc/fixcorr.rmd
as.theta.vcov <- function(Sigma,corrs.only=FALSE) {
    logsd <- log(diag(Sigma))/2
    cr <- cov2cor(Sigma)
    cc <- chol(cr)
    cc <- cc %*% diag(1 / diag(cc))
    corrs <- cc[upper.tri(cc)]
    if (corrs.only) return(corrs)
    ret <- c(logsd,corrs)
    return(ret)
}

correlation_matrix = vcv(phyl.upd2)[unique(data$Species), unique(data$Species)]

###
#the following code was taken from https://github.com/glmmTMB/glmmTMB/blob/master/misc/fixcorr.rmd
as.theta.vcov <- function(Sigma,corrs.only=FALSE) {
    logsd <- log(diag(Sigma))/2
    cr <- cov2cor(Sigma)
    cc <- chol(cr)
    cc <- cc %*% diag(1 / diag(cc))
    corrs <- cc[upper.tri(cc)]
    if (corrs.only) return(corrs)
    ret <- c(logsd,corrs)
    return(ret)
}
corrs = as.theta.vcov(correlation_matrix, corrs.only=TRUE)

title: Appendix C — Case studies
text:
C.6 Snouter









CautionTasks



Fit one of the (continuous) responses in the snouter dataset, e.g. snouter1.1, against the predictors rain + djungle (see ?snouter); the coordinates are X and Y. Check for spatial autocorrelation and proceed to fitting a spatial model if needed (Section 11.3). See the data set’s help for details on the variables.



library(EcoData)
str(snouter)







TipSolution





Fit a base model, then check its residuals for spatial autocorrelation. We use snouter1.1 (a continuous response) here; the coordinates in this dataset are X and Y:

library(EcoData); library(glmmTMB); library(DHARMa)
fit = glmmTMB(snouter1.1 ~ rain + djungle, data = snouter)
res = simulateResiduals(fit); plot(res)







testSpatialAutocorrelation(res, x = snouter$X, y = snouter$Y)









    DHARMa Moran's I test for distance-based autocorrelation

data:  res
observed = 0.12556787, expected = -0.00090334, sd = 0.00141608, p-value
< 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: Distance-based autocorrelation


If the spatial test is significant, we first de-trend with a 2D spline (as recommended in Section 11.1.1 - always de-trend before reaching for a correlation structure):

library(mgcv)
fit2 = gam(snouter1.1 ~ rain + djungle + te(X, Y), data = snouter)
res2 = simulateResiduals(fit2)
testSpatialAutocorrelation(res2, x = snouter$X, y = snouter$Y)









    DHARMa Moran's I test for distance-based autocorrelation

data:  res2
observed = 0.03162372, expected = -0.00090334, sd = 0.00141607, p-value
< 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: Distance-based autocorrelation


This changes residuals somewhat, but there is still significant spatial autocorrelation left. Thus, we have to move to a spatial model.

title: Appendix C — Case studies
text:
C.7 Volcano Island









CautionTasks



Analyze ?volcanoisland in the EcoData package. Perform an appropriate causal statistical analysis (see Chapter 7; including residual checks and everything) to understand the predictors that determine the value of

windObs (numeric)
lizards (1/0)
beetles2 (counts)
survivedOf20 (k out of 20)

There are various predictors, including plot, year, x, y that can be considered. Assume that all the issues that we talked about (random effects, Chapter 4; overdispersion, Section 9.3.2; zero-inflation, Section 9.3.3; spatial autocorrelation, Section 11.3) could appear in this data.
Hint: it is possible that the possibility to observe a species depends on wind, and it is possible that lizards eat beetles, so you can also consider these variables (or predictions for these variables) as predictors of the others.
Hint 2: binomial k/n data in R is specified as a response that is cbind(k, n-k), so you would write glm(cbind(survivedOf20, 20 - survivedOf20) ~ predictor, data = data, family = “binomial”)
Hint 3: lizards may be present but not observed (imperfect detection, see Hint 1). Occupancy models, which separate the true presence from the detection process, are introduced with the same data set in the chapter on occupancy models of Hartig (2024).



Hartig, F. (2024) “Introduction to Bayesian statistics with R.” Available at: https://florianhartig.github.io/LearningBayes/.






TipSolution





Base model
This is an open, integrative exercise, so the following is not a fully worked-out solution but a base model to start from for one of the responses (beetle counts). The other responses (windObs -> Gaussian / gls, lizards -> binomial, survivedOf20 -> k/n binomial) follow exactly the same recipe.

library(EcoData); library(glmmTMB); library(DHARMa)
d = volcanoisland

# beetles: counts -> start with Poisson and plot as RE, then diagnose
m0 = glmmTMB(beetles2 ~ windObs + lizards + (1|plot), family = poisson, data = d)
res = simulateResiduals(m0); plot(res)







testDispersion(res); testZeroInflation(res)









    DHARMa nonparametric dispersion test via sd of residuals fitted vs.
    simulated

data:  simulationOutput
dispersion = 2.6752, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: two.sided










    DHARMa zero-inflation test via comparison to expected zeros with
    simulation under H0 = fitted model

data:  simulationOutput
ratioObsSim = 1.1159, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: two.sided

# if over-dispersed / zero-inflated -> negative binomial + ZI term
m1 = glmmTMB(beetles2 ~ windObs + lizards + (1|plot),
             family = nbinom2, ziformula = ~1, data = d)

# then check for residual spatial autocorrelation on the coordinates
res1 = simulateResiduals(m1)
grp  = recalculateResiduals(res1, group = d$plot)
testSpatialAutocorrelation(grp,
      x = aggregate(x ~ plot, d, mean)$x,
      y = aggregate(y ~ plot, d, mean)$y)









    DHARMa Moran's I test for distance-based autocorrelation

data:  grp
observed = 0.205367, expected = -0.010101, sd = 0.017216, p-value <
2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: Distance-based autocorrelation


Work through the diagnostic ladder (Table 12.3) in order - functional form -> distribution -> dispersion -> zero-inflation -> correlation - adding structure only when a residual check demands it. Note the hint that lizards (predators) may belong in the beetle model, and that detectability may depend on windObs.
